sources.news_title: Americans vote for new Congress members in US midterm election
sources.text:
Millions of Americans are voting at polling stations across the United States to elect new members of Congress in the country’s midterm elections.
The election is expected to play a major role in shaping the nation’s political direction and the balance of power in Washington.
American voters are choosing representatives for all 435 seats in the House of Representatives, alongside 35 seats in the Senate, including two special elections.
Several states are also holding gubernatorial elections.
|  |  | 
|---|---|
The election comes at a critical moment for President Donald Trump‘s administration as Republican and Democratic parties compete to secure control of Congress for the remaining two years of his presidential term.
Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate. They also hold a slim majority in the House of Representatives. However, Democrats hope to gain enough seats to take control of both the Senate and the House.
Among the most closely watched races are Senate seats in Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, and Texas.

Whichever party controls Congress will determine the balance of power in Washington. The midterm results affect the legislative agenda and control of congressional committees.
A Republican majority in both houses of Congress would give President Donald Trump an easier path to enact his desired agenda for the remainder of his term.
If Democrats take back a majority in either or both chambers, they can have a greater say in the nation’s laws,
US President Donald Trump has campaigned for weeks for Americans to vote Republican.
PREMIUM TIMES reported that in September, he promised to pay every adult American $5,000 if Republicans retain control of Congress.

However, Republicans worry that Mr Trump’s deep unpopularity could affect how the party fares in the election. His unpopularity is driven by discontent over inflation and high consumer and gas prices.
It has also been linked to the trade war with China and Canada. There are also concerns about the US war with Iran.
Mr Trump, on Tuesday, labelled the upcoming midterm elections as the most important “in our lifetime.”
He also labelled the Democratic candidates “the most extreme and dangerous” list of candidates in the country’s history.

sources.news_title: US midterm elections 2026: Voting begins as Trump’s policies face public test
sources.text:
US citizens began voting on Tuesday in the midterm elections, which are being closely watched around the world as the results could reflect public opinion on President Donald Trump and his policies. Trump’s decisions, including the tariff war and the ongoing Gulf conflict, have had a major impact on the global economy in recent months.
According to the IANS, Trump described the elections as the “most important midterm I believe in our lifetime” during his final campaign rally on Monday.
Advertisement
The first voters entered polling booths in Vermont at 5 am local time (3:30 pm IST). Voting will continue across the country, with Alaska being the last state to close its polling stations at 9 pm local time (11:30 am Wednesday in India).
As of Monday evening, around 57 million of the 174 million eligible voters had already cast their votes through mail-in ballots or early voting centres. The remaining voters are casting their ballots on Tuesday.
US Midterm Elections: Voting Across States, Early Results Expected
The first indications of the election trends may emerge around midnight in Washington (10:30 am Wednesday in India). However, the final results could take days or even weeks due to recounts and legal challenges.
Some technical problems were also reported during voting. In Westchester County, north of New York City, voting machines stopped working, forcing officials to ask voters to submit paper ballots.
Trump’s name does not appear on the ballots for the 435 House of Representatives seats, 35 Senate seats, 36 governor posts and thousands of state and local legislative positions.
However, Trump has made the elections a test of his presidency by repeatedly asking voters to consider him a candidate. “Pretend I am on the ballot,” he has told voters during his campaign.
Most opinion polls predict that the Democrats could win control of the House of Representatives, while the contest for the Senate remains uncertain.
Trump appeared to acknowledge the possibility of a setback during his final campaign rally on Monday. “For some reason, the sitting President doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot,” he said.
He campaigned across 20 states, holding 30 rallies over 32 days. Most of his campaign events were held in Republican-dominated states, also known as ‘red states’, indicating his focus on retaining support among Republican voters.
Trump’s Policies And Economic Concerns Under Scrutiny
The elections are taking place amid growing concerns over the economy and rising living costs. The Gulf conflict, which has contributed to higher prices of everyday goods and fuel, has also affected Trump’s political standing.
On Monday, the United States carried out what it described as a “small-scale defensive measure” against missile targets on Iran’s Qeshm Island.
Although the US economy grew by 3.4 per cent in the latest quarter, inflation stood at 3.7 per cent in September. Rising prices of food and other essential goods have increased pressure on households.
Opinion polls indicate a decline in Trump’s popularity. He won the 2024 presidential election with 49.8 per cent of the votes. However, the RealClearPolitics (RCP) average of polls now shows Democrats leading the congressional election preference with 52.1 per cent support.
According to the RCP figures, Trump’s job approval rating has fallen from 50.3 per cent during the first week of his second term to 39.1 per cent. Meanwhile, his disapproval rating has increased to 58.8 per cent.
The election results will determine how these polling trends translate into seats in Congress and whether the Democrats can gain control of either chamber.

US Voters Head to Polls for Midterm Elections
Error: Contact form not found.
by Reuters and Algemeiner Staff
Americans headed to the polls in Tuesday’s midterm elections to deliver a verdict on the first two years of President Donald Trump‘s second term, with surveys and nonpartisan analysts favoring Democrats to wrest the House of Representatives from Republicans while control of the Senate remains uncertain.
The battle for the Senate is unfolding across nearly 10 closely contested statewide races, most in Republican strongholds.
History is against Trump‘s Republicans: The sitting president’s party has lost ground in Congress in all but two midterm elections since World War Two. Trump‘s approval rating is hovering near his all-time lows, dragged down in part by voter frustration over the rise in fuel prices sparked by the war with Iran.
Much of this year’s election is about Trump, the central US political figure for most of the last decade. Trump himself has told his supporters repeatedly to “pretend I’m on the ballot” to motivate high Republican voter turnout, a message that Democratic leaders have echoed to ensure their own electoral base shows up to vote.
Trump, in a television interview on Tuesday morning, boasted of what he billed as his achievements in Venezuela and Iran and declared optimism for fellow Republicans.
“I think the results are going to be better than you think,” he told Fox News, adding that he would be watching the results come in later Tuesday night at the White House, where he is hosting a viewing reception.
In remarks that appeared aimed at swaying largely Democratic-leaning voters unhappy with US support for Israel, the lone democracy in the Middle East and a critical strategic ally, Trump said that Washington would stop $4 billion in annual funding to the country after the end of this year.
US policy toward Israel has been a particular focus in Michigan, where progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is running a closely watched campaign for Senate.
The president has sought to energize his base with more than two dozen campaign rallies since the start of October, the vast majority in states he easily won in 2024, underscoring the extent to which Republicans are playing defense.
Led by Trump, Republicans have portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, un-American, and even communist.
“The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history,” Trump said on Monday during a speech in Washington.
However, opinion polls show voters are most concerned about affordability and disapprove of Trump‘s handling of the issue, after his sweeping tariff policy and his decision to attack Iran in February increased domestic costs. Republican candidates, meanwhile, have struggled in some swing states to distance themselves from a president who places high value on loyalty.
All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives are up for election, along with 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats, though the majority of contests are not considered competitive. Democrats must flip at least three House seats and four Senate seats to win a majority in each chamber.
Democrats have little margin for error. The party must defend all of its current seats while winning at least two states that voted for Trump by a double-digit margin two years ago: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas.
Opinion polls show Democrats either narrowly leading or within striking distance in all of those states.
MICHIGAN RACE ROILED BY CROSS-PARTY ENDORSEMENT
The Michigan Senate contest between El-Sayed, 42, and Republican former US Representative Mike Rogers, 63, received a fresh jolt on Sunday when Democrat Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in the party’s primary election, endorsed Rogers in a surprise reversal.
In addition to the implications for Senate control, the Michigan race represents a high-profile test case of whether a battleground state will elect a far-left candidate who Republicans and some independents and moderate Democrats accuse of holding extreme positions.
A win for El-Sayed, who has regularly attacked Israel and supports liberal policies such as universal healthcare, would be seen as a boost for the party’s left wing ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
The Alaska Senate race has been caught up in its own turmoil, after the New York Times reported that the campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, 53, helped recruit a third candidate who shares the first and last name of her Republican opponent, Dan Sullivan, 61.
Peltola has denied involvement. Trump‘s Justice Department has launched a criminal probe into the allegations and filed a lawsuit to block certification of the election results, though a judge dismissed the latter effort.
In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, 37, has his party once again dreaming of winning the biggest Republican state after decades of heartbreak. His scandal-plagued opponent, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, 63, has benefited from a nine-figure investment from the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, who has spent hundreds of millions of dollars boosting Republicans.
In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton, 62, a megachurch pastor, holds a narrow polling lead over Republican US Senator Roger Marshall, 66. The state voted for Trump by more than 16 percentage points in 2024 and has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century.
And in Maine, Republican US Senator Susan Collins, 73, is once again seeking to defy the Democratic leanings of her home state and win a sixth term. She faces Democrat Troy Jackson, 58, a former state senate president who unexpectedly became the nominee after Democratic oyster farmer Graham Platner dropped out amid accusations of misconduct, which he denied.
Other competitive Senate races are taking place in Iowa, Nebraska, Ohio, and South Carolina, all Republican-held seats.
TRUMP‘S JUSTICE DEPARTMENT INTERVENES
The US Justice Department said on Tuesday it was deploying 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states in what it called the largest Election Day monitoring effort in history.
Department officials have said priorities include areas with a history of voter access issues and places with competitive races that could be targets of voter intimidation.
There are 47 US House races widely seen as competitive, according to a Reuters analysis of the leading election forecasters. If the other contests all proceed as predicted, Democrats would need to win only 13 of the competitive races to secure a majority.
The fight for the House has been waged largely on Republican turf, including some districts Trump carried by double digits in 2024. A Trump-backed Republican effort to redraw districts in several states to make them safer for the party appears not to have yielded the gains the White House expected.
In addition to its actions in Alaska, Trump‘s Justice Department also filed a lawsuit in California to block ballots it says may be invalid, a break from decades of practice meant to insulate elections from political influence. The US Supreme Court on Monday rejected the administration’s request for an emergency order in the case.
Three dozen governors’ races will also take place on Tuesday, as well as thousands of state-level legislative contests and ballot measures on issues from a billionaires’ tax to abortion rights.

sources.text:
As Election Day arrives, Democrats poised to see gains and pump brakes on Trump agenda
Early voting at Kearny Town Hall in Kearny, New Jersey, on Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
WASHINGTON — Tens of millions of Americans have already cast a ballot in the 2026 midterm elections that will determine control of Congress and shape President Donald Trump’s remaining policy agenda.
As of Monday, more than 57 million Americans had cast a vote, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, which tracks early voting. This year’s elections have already shattered the record for midterm early voting, set in 2022, in which nearly 46 million Americans voted early.
Polls close between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m. local time on Election Day. Under federal law, as long as voters are in line when the polls close, they can still cast their ballots. Voters must be at least 18 years old, a U.S. citizen and registered to vote in their state. Many states allow same-day registration.
Trump came into his second term with his party in control of both chambers of Congress. But historically, the president’s party loses seats in the midterm elections, and this cycle appears unlikely to be an exception.
Elections forecasters have favored Democrats to win back the majority in the U.S. House, which would allow them to significantly rein in Trump’s legislative agenda. Analysts have also increasingly predicted Democrats could win control of the U.S. Senate could, which would allow them to block appointments, including a potential U.S. Supreme Court vacancy.
The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter projects Democrats to pick up a Senate seat in North Carolina and lists six more races as toss-ups, all of which are now held by Republicans. Those races are in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio and Texas. Democrats are defending an open seat in Michigan that the Cook Political Report moved from toss-up to leaning toward the Democrat, Abdul El-Sayed, on Monday.
If the other races go as predicted, Democrats would have to win at least three of the toss-ups to gain control of the chamber.
The Cook Political Report shifted 12 House races in the direction of Democrats on Oct. 30. Eighteen remained toss-ups as of Monday. Democrats have to net three seats to flip control of the House, if they also win the race in a heavily Democratic Florida district that is vacant after former Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick resigned in April.
If Democrats gain the majority in the House, they are likely to pursue investigations into Trump and other administration officials.
They have also signaled they will embrace a policy agenda centered on lowering costs, especially related to healthcare, though Trump’s veto looms on any major legislation Congress passes for the next two years.
Legal challenges amid dismal numbers
The war with Iran that has contributed to high gas and diesel prices, inflation and an aggressive immigration crackdown has led to historically low presidential approval ratings. Trump’s approval on average was at 37% Monday, only a tick better than his second-term low of 36% recorded just two weeks earlier, according to The New York Times.
The president has already made an attempt to use the Department of Justice to halt the certification of the Alaska U.S. Senate race, after The New York Times reported the campaign of Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola made an effort to recruit a candidate with the same name as GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan in order to stack the four-way general election in her favor.
States Newsroom has not independently verified the Times story.
A federal judge tossed out the lawsuit Sunday.
Other court challenges related to the administration’s actions or potential actions related to the election are still unfolding on Election Day. Cases include Democrats’ aim to bar armed federal officials for polling locations and DOJ’s effort to prevent California from counting 20,000 votes the Trump administration suspects are noncitizens.
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday denied the Trump administration’s final attempt to force California to set aside the ballots.
Separately, congressional Democrats have taken their own precautions. More than 100 Senate staffers and 300 House staffers were trained as election monitors and will be sent to 60 or 70 close races, the top Democrat on the House Administration Committee, Joe Morelle, told reporters last week.
Even after the polls close, it could take weeks to know the results of some races, and consequently, control of both chambers of Congress, due to each state’s voting laws and processes for counting votes.
After the 2022 midterms, control of the House was projected for Republicans eight days after Election Day. In 2024, the same projection took nine days.

sources.news_title: Bemidji area voters head to the polls for 2026 midterm election
sources.text:
BEMIDJI — Polling places across the region were hustling and bustling on Tuesday morning with voters casting their ballots in the midterm election.
This election marks a first for residents of Northern Township as it moves to become an official city once its first Northern City Council is sworn in on Nov. 23. Seats up for election on Tuesday include mayor and two two-year and two four-year at-large council seats, to create staggered elections.
ADVERTISEMENT
For Bemidji area voters, the ballot includes options for Ward 2, Ward 4 and At-Large seats on the Bemidji City Council, District 1 on the Beltrami County Board of Commissioners and five candidates running for three seats on the Bemidji school board.
Regional races include House 2A and 2B, Senate District 2 and Congressional District 8. Statewide races include Governor, Secretary of State, Auditor, Attorney General and U.S. Senator.
There is also a constitutional amendment on the ballot that, if passed, would change the annual funding distribution from public land held in trust for Minnesota public schools from 2.5% to 4.5% annually.
A lack of response to the question — Shall the Minnesota Constitution be amended to increase the funding going to all school districts from the permanent school fund, which is a fund that supports school districts without raising individual income or property taxes, effective July 1, 2027? — counts as a "no" vote; if residents support the amendment, they should vote "yes."
There are also a handful of local races up for election where candidates are running unopposed, including Beltrami County Attorney, Auditor/Treasurer, Commissioner District 3, Sheriff, Soil and Water Supervisor District 1 and Soil and Water Supervisor District 2. Numerous court and judge positions are also up for election with candidates running unopposed.
To see a full sample ballot for your ward or township, visit myballotmn.sos.mn.gov.
Polling locations are open until 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3. Voters who are in line before 8 p.m. will still be allowed to cast their ballots, even if they haven't reached the front by closing time.
ADVERTISEMENT
For those unsure of where to vote, information is available on the county’s website or through the Minnesota poll finder at pollfinder.sos.state.mn.us.
City of Bemidji polling places are dictated by ward of residence:
- Ward 1: Northwest Indian Community Development Center at 1819 Bemidji Ave. N.
- Ward 2: Bemidji National Guard Armory at 1430 23rd St. NW.
- Ward 3: Boys and Girls Club at 1600 Minnesota Ave. NW.
- Ward 4: City Hall at 317 Fourth St. NW.
- Ward 5: Northwest Technical College, commons area at 905 Grant Ave. SE.
According to the Secretary of State, as of 9 a.m. on Monday, Nov. 2, local election officials had accepted 886,427 absentee and mail ballots for the midterm election. Of the accepted ballots, 266,580 were returned by mail and 619,847 ballots were cast in person.
This is the highest number of absentee and mail ballots cast before an election in a non-presidential election year. Additional absentee voting statistics are available online.
For up-to-date election stories and results, visit the Election 2026 section at bemidjipioneer.com.

sources.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/live-updates-midterm-voters-go-to-the-polls-on-election-day Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Live Updates: First Senate race call gives Democrats a win in Virginia Politics Updated on Nov 3, 2026 7:53 PM EST — Published on Nov 3, 2026 11:00 AM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check Election Day is here. Voters nationwide will decide control of the U.S. House and Senate. Democrats must flip four seats in the Senate and three seats in the House to wrest control of the chambers from Republicans. Control of Congress would give Democrats a way to push back against President Donald Trump's agenda during the final two years of his term. The battle for control is playing out mostly in states and districts Trump previously won by wide margins. WATCH LIVE: Election night 2026 PBS News special coverage All eyes are on Senate contests in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas, while House battlegrounds are scattered across the country. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Democrats have homed in on Trump's poor approval rating, public dissatisfaction with the war in Iran and affordability concerns. Republicans have focused on social issues, while Trump has made himself the central character of the midterms. Here's the latest. 7:53 p.m. EST Black voter turnout appears robust on Election Day, voter coalition says LaTosha Brown, co-founder of the voting rights group Black Voters Matter, said turnout in some states seemed to rival that of 2008, when Democrat Barack Obama was running for president for the first time. She and others said turnout appeared particularly high in Michigan and Mississippi. Brown, speaking during a media briefing organized by the National Coalition on Black Civic Participation, said her organization had more than 2,000 poll observers in several states. They reported no "widescale issues" for voters, she said. Melanie Campbell, president and CEO of the coalition, said the group has extended its monitoring efforts beyond Election Day — through vote counting, certifications and even winners' inaugurations. "As those of us who believe that this democracy is for all people, we have to also stand in the gap," she said. 7:33 p.m. EST Civil rights group says ICE social media message intended to intimidate voters Carmen Feliciano, vice president for policy and advocacy at the Latino civil rights group UnidosUS, criticized U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for a social media post that said, in part: "If you vote illegally, we will find you." The agency posted the message on Election Day. "This is part of a strategy we have been seeing for the last few years — intimidation and trying to block people from going out to the polls," Feliciano said. She noted that Latino turnout was expected to be high for the midterm elections. Asked why the message went out, the Department of Homeland Security, which includes ICE, issued a statement that read in part: "ONLY Americans should elect American leaders." Throughout the day, ICE announced arrests or charges against people suspected of voting as noncitizens in previous elections. 7:14 p.m. EST Key U.S. House races to watch in Florida A handful of key U.S. House races in Florida could offer early signs of how Democrats are performing tonight. LIVE RESULTS: Florida Senate midterm election Democratic Reps. Darren Soto and Kathy Castor are defending their seats in the redrawn 9th and 14th Districts. Both of the districts would have favored Trump by double-digit margins in the 2024 presidential election. The 22nd District is an open seat after Democratic Rep. Lois Frankel opted to run in the 23rd District when her district was redrawn. What to watch for after polls close at 7 p.m. ET All polls close at 7 p.m. in six states, including Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia, which tend to complete almost all of their vote counting on election night. READ MORE: Here's when polls are closing in each state this midterm election In the 2024 general election, the vote count in all three states reached the halfway mark in the 8 p.m. hour. The counts were 90% complete at 10:21 p.m. in Georgia, 11:14 p.m. in South Carolina and 12:07 a.m. in Virginia. In Georgia's competitive presidential contest, The Associated Press declared Trump the winner at 12:58 a.m. Democratic and Republican observers review ballots during midterm elections at the Fulton County Election Hub and Operation Center in Fairburn, Georgia, Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Edgar Su/Reuters Most Florida polls will also close at 7 p.m., including in every competitive congressional district, but no statewide winners will be declared until polls in the Central Time Zone close at 8 p.m. Polls in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia close at 7:30 p.m. All three states also count votes relatively quickly, reaching the halfway point at around 9 p.m. in 2024 and about 90% in the 11 p.m. hour. The AP declared a winner in Ohio's competitive 2024 U.S. Senate race at 11:27 p.m. Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio; gubernatorial races in Georgia and Ohio; and U.S. House races in Florida, Indiana, South Carolina, Virginia, Ohio and North Carolina. 6:52 p.m. EST Flooding strands voters on the Navajo Nation Hundreds of voters in Rock Point, Arizona, on the Navajo Nation were unable to reach the polls Tuesday as flooding had closed a major bridge and washed out dirt roads, a tribal official said. On a typical Election Day, the chapter house parking lot would be buzzing with voters, candidates and pop-up food stalls. "Unfortunately, today that parking lot is underwater," said Valinda Shirley, vice president of the Rock Point Chapter, the local seat of tribal government. Officials moved the polling place across the street to an administration building, but many residents remained stranded. "I have people that are still texting me asking how I can get them out so they can vote," Shirley said Tuesday afternoon. The flooding is keeping those residents from casting ballots in both the U.S. midterms and races for Navajo Nation president and council delegates. 6:38 p.m. EST Jeffries says House Democrats are ready to deliver the 'best version' of America Jeffries, who's in line to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if Democrats seize control and elect him to the job, said House Democrats don't work for any president. "We work for all of you, the American people, and we're committed to delivering an America that's the best version of herself," he said. He told the volunteers that Democrats are "committed to ending this national nightmare, fighting to make this country affordable" and "continuing our country's long, necessary and majestic march toward a more perfect union." He urged them on: "Let's go win this thing." 6:11 p.m. EST Jeffries says Democrats 'on the brink' of taking back the House House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries popped by to rally and thank volunteers at a phone bank in Washington for battleground House candidates. "We're on the brink of a dramatic change in the direction in the country," Jeffries said. "We're on the brink of Democrats taking back control of the House of Representatives." He said a Democratic win would be a victory for Americans. "We're going to deliver a Congress that actually puts the American people first," he said. Volunteers applaud as House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries gives two thumbs at a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) midterm election night phone bank and watch party at a hotel in Washington, D.C., Nov. 3, 2026. Kansas voter trusts Trump will bring fuel prices down Daryl Compton, a 73-year-old retired UPS worker, attended a rally in Topeka, Kansas, last week headlined by Vice President Vance wearing a red "Make America Great Again" cap. Compton said he's concerned about illegal immigration, the economy and national security, particularly the threat posed by Iran. He also said fuel prices are too high, "but I put my trust in Trump that they are going to come down." LIVE RESULTS: Kansas Senate midterm election "And I think they'll come down a lot further than we even expect," he said. Compton said he's motivated to vote for Republican Sen. Roger Marshall because if Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton wins, that could put Democrats in charge of the Senate. "I don't like Democrats," he said. "They're basically not Democrats. They are more like Communists, and I'm against Communism." Voting in one Florida county delayed due to bar code issue as polls open Voting was delayed for 20 minutes at voting sites across Broward County as polls opened because a new safety feature malfunctioned, officials said. During a news conference, Supervisor of Elections Joe Scott apologized to voters who had to wait and said some left before they were able to vote. The problem was solved by 7:20 a.m., and Scott encouraged those who left to return. He did not have an estimate of how many voters left. Scott said the state's late redistricting meant some people within the same precinct voted on different ballots, and the new bar code feature was meant to ensure poll workers did not give people the wrong one. Some people received an error message that they were voting on the wrong ballot, but they were not, Scott said. "Nobody voted on the wrong ballot," Scott said. "None of the counts were impacted." Millions of voters face new laws at ballot box More than three dozen voting laws passed in Republican-controlled states are taking effect for the first time this year, many of them containing elements of proposals that Trump tried unsuccessfully to get through Congress. At the state level, the changes include new requirements to show proof of citizenship. College students in New Hampshire won't be using college IDs. Iowa voters without ID can't count on other voters to vouch for them, and some voters in Mississippi might need birth certificates or passports for verification. Naturalized citizens might get to polling places and learn they've been purged because databases used to check their citizenship against voter registration lists are outdated. READ MORE: 5 expert takeaways on 2026 midterm election security Opponents say the restrictions make it harder for eligible voters to vote. Republican lawmakers who support the tighter voting laws, especially around voter ID, say they help build trust in elections. The Texas governor's race has focused on a new lightning rod: data centers A campaign sign for Democratic Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa near a polling station during the midterm elections, on Election Day, in Austin, Texas, Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Mike Segar/ Reuters Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who has comfortably held the governor's mansion since 2014, is in one of his tougher fights. He faces Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa in an election year favoring her party. The race, still an uphill slog for Hinojosa, has revolved around the standard concerns of high costs and public education, but the hulking structures that power artificial intelligence butted in. Data centers have drawn bipartisan anger from Americans who live by them and concerns that the buildings guzzle too much water and electricity. Last year, Abbott celebrated Google's investments partly to build data centers in the state. Hinojosa hammered him for it, arguing that it represented the influence of wealthy people over everyday Texans. The governor has since shifted his position, ordering the pause of data center permits and saying, "Texans come first." 11:11 a.m. EST Flooding prompts relocation of some polling places in Florida Some voters in Florida were being directed to cast their ballots in new places on Tuesday after their polling sites were relocated due to continued rain and flooding. Florida elections officials said 21 polling places in eight counties were moved. The relocations were mostly along the central and southern Atlantic coast, with some inland counties included. County officials said they notified voters by text and email, and signs were posted at voting locations directing people to the new sites. Some residents expressed frustration and concern on social media that some voters may not be able to get to the polls because of flooding. Amy Keith, the Florida state director for Common Cause, said the flooding is a big issue. "Today it has already been a pretty challenging morning," she said, urging voters to double-check their voting locations with election supervisors. Schumer says he's 'nauseously optimistic' After casting his vote at a Brooklyn school, Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer said he was optimistic that when polls close, "there will be a new Democratic majority in the United States Senate." "We don't want to count our chickens before they hatch. So I'd characterize our mood as nauseously optimistic," Schumer said. He predicted that Democrat Abdul El-Sayed would win the U.S. Senate race in Michigan, despite the decision by his former primary opponent, U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, to endorse Republican Mike Rogers. WATCH LIVE: House Democratic Leader Jeffries holds Election Day news conference "She's one vote," Schumer said. "He's going to win tonight because he's talking about what Michiganders care about." Schumer said that a year ago, no one thought the Democrats might be in a position to retake the Senate. But he credited the party's "relentless" focus on affordability and "chaos overseas in a war with Iran that nobody wants" with making Democrats more competitive. A look at recent midterm election results Midterm elections generally favor the party that doesn't hold the White House, but the two most recent cycles generated a mixed result. When Joe Biden was president, Republicans won control of the House in 2022, picking up nine seats and assuming a slim majority. But Democrats maintained control of the Senate and even picked up a seat in the chamber. A similar dynamic occurred during Trump's first term, though the gains were much larger for Democrats in the House. They netted 40 seats in the 2018 midterms and took the majority for the first time in eight years. Still, Republicans expanded their Senate majority by two seats. Some analysts see similarities between this midterm political environment and that of 2006, when President George W. Bush and Republicans faced headwinds from high fuel prices and the war in Iraq. That year, Democrats added 30 House seats and six Senate seats to take the majority in both chambers. 10:36 a.m. EST Massive spending and presidential visits signal Ohio is back in play After years of having its storied bellwether status written off, Ohio is competitive again. Republicans should have run away with critical contests for U.S. Senate and governor, based on Trump's three consecutive sweeping victories in the state. Instead, they headed into Election Day in close contests with their Democratic rivals. WATCH: Campaigns spend big to sway voters with increasingly personal attack ads Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown has mounted a comeback bid against Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, appointed last year to the seat formerly held by Vice President JD Vance. Both Trump and Vance visited Ohio in the campaign's closing weeks to rally voters, as did former President Barack Obama for Democrats. The governor's contest pits Republican biotech entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy against Democrat Dr. Amy Acton, the state's former COVID-era health director. An ad Ramaswamy ran featuring Acton's estranged mother became a flashpoint in the race and across the U.S. Ukraine's Zelenskyy warns of massive Russian strikes as the world focuses on U.S. midterms Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Russia will step up massive drone and missile strikes on his country's energy facilities this week while international attention is focused on the U.S. midterm elections. "The world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defense and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked," he said in an evening video post. Russian ballistic missiles and drones damaged energy facilities in 10 Ukrainian regions Tuesday — part of a campaign by Moscow to pressure Kyiv over the winter months. General mood of the country from AP-NORC polling Americans have been in a sour mood about the country's direction for several years, according to AP-NORC polling. About 7 in 10 U.S. adults say the country is heading in the wrong direction, according to AP-NORC polling from September. Only about one-quarter of U.S. adults say things are headed in the "right direction." Democrats and independents are much likelier than Republicans to say things are not going the right way. READ MORE: Election Day underway after a surge in early voting, as Trump sows doubt on results Roughly 6 in 10 U.S. adults say they are feeling "very" or "somewhat" pessimistic about the state of politics in this country, according to an AP-NORC poll from October. About half are feeling negatively about the future of democracy in the U.S. U.S. will halt $4B in aid to Israel as ally shifts to buying military hardware, Trump says The Republican president told Fox News Channel during an Election Day telephone interview that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple of years. Trump said Israel doesn't need the aid and that it's a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also said the aid had become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. READ MORE: Trump says U.S. will stop giving $4 billion in aid to Israel next year "We give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don't need it," Trump said. Netanyahu's office had no immediate comment. The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over the past few years. Trump has spent months trying to overhaul how U.S. elections work, without much success This year's midterm elections are being run by state and local officials, in much the way they've always done it — but that's not for lack of trying by Trump. The Republican president has been trying to expand his influence over the way U.S. elections operate ever since returning to office, largely unsuccessfully, through executive action, lawsuits and legislation. READ MORE: What to look for on Election Day as questions loom over Trump The Supreme Court in September closed the chapter on one of his boldest efforts — a plan that would have demanded a dramatic overhaul of the nation's mail voting processes. Trump also failed this year to coerce the Republican-led Senate to pass his SAVE America Act, which would have required documentary proof of citizenship for anyone registering to vote. Still, some of his administration's efforts have succeeded in reshaping the midterms, including a redistricting push that convinced multiple Republican-led states to pass partisan congressional maps to minimize potential losses. Trump says midterm results will be 'better than you think' Trump says Tuesday's midterm results will be "better than you think" for Republicans, declaring that "inflation is solved" and "everything's going good." Trump's closing day message conflicts with frustration many voters are feeling with the economy, as the cost of groceries, gas and healthcare has climbed despite the president's promise to bring down prices. READ MORE: 3 things to watch on election night (and beyond) Inflation is running at 3.7% annually, up from 3% when Trump's second term started. Trump didn't acknowledge concerns about prices in his Tuesday morning interview with "Fox and Friends." Instead, he touted his administration's immigration enforcement and said U.S. manufacturing was expanding. "I think the results are going to be better than you think," he said. Talarico takes Democrats' biggest swing in years at winning Texas Texas hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1988, but the party is brimming with hope that it has the perfect storm to do so this year: a well-spoken candidate in James Talarico, an opponent saddled with scandals in Republican Ken Paxton, and an election favoring Democrats nationwide. Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian and state lawmaker, has focused on Texans' struggles against everyday costs, which he squarely blames on uber-wealthy people corrupting politics. Paxton, Talarico argues, is the flag-bearer of that corruption. LIVE FACT CHECK: Election Day 2026 Paxton is the Lone Star State's longtime attorney general and conservative culture warrior. He's lived under a cloud of ethical questions, which led to his own party impeaching him on corruption allegations in the statehouse. Paxton has repeatedly hammered Talarico on his past statements, including "God is nonbinary," insisting that he's too "woke" for Texas. Voting continues in suburban county outside New York City, despite machine issue Voters in Westchester County continue to cast ballots at polling locations despite a countywide issue with machines that aren't accepting paper ballots. The Westchester County Board of Elections said ballots are being placed in designated orange emergency ballot bags as they resolve the issue. The board said the ballots would remain secure and monitored and would be counted. Some voters in the county are deciding a competitive U.S. House race between Rep. Mike Lawler and his Democratic opponent, Cait Conley. Both candidates posted statements on X, urging voters to stay in line. State Attorney General Letitia James said her office is in contact with state and local election officials. The county includes the cities of Yonkers and White Plains. It is located north of Manhattan along the Hudson River and has more than 1 million residents. Paxton's past split this Texas couple's vote Liz Tabor, 62, and her husband, Mark Bauer, 59, cast their early vote for Republicans at Buda City Hall in Texas, though Tabor's GOP ticket had a few exceptions. "I did not vote for Paxton," she said of the Republican Senate candidate, who was impeached by his own party but acquitted and has faced allegations of extramarital affairs. "I just can't. There's so much with his past." "It's an accumulation of his shady behavior," she added. LIVE RESULTS: Texas Senate midterm election She didn't vote for his Democratic rival, though, either. She instead opted for the Libertarian candidate. Bauer voted for Paxton, saying it was more important to have a Republican in office. The two have lived in Texas for 26 years and said that what Republicans have done at the border is a good thing, and that they hoped to see more of it. The nation's longest Senate winning streak is at stake in Kansas Jonathan, 4, watches as his mom votes at a polling station during the midterm elections on Election Day in Overland Park, Kansas, on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Nathan Howard/ Reuters Sen. Roger Marshall is trying to fend off an unusually strong challenge from Democratic megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton in a race that's generated a Kansas record for spending on advertising. A Democrat hasn't won a Senate race in the state in 94 years. But Marshall is seeking a second term at a moment of deep frustration with Trump's handling of the economy, and Hamilton made affordability a key issue while positioning himself as a moderate who could work with Republican colleagues in Washington. Hamilton is the founder and senior pastor of the Kansas City-area Church of the Resurrection. With 25,000 members, it's the nation's largest United Methodist congregation. DeSantis urges Trump, Republicans not to 'gaslight' voters In a Monday interview with commentator Stephen A. Smith, Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Trump originally promised not to start new wars in the Middle East, but is currently in an "open-ended" conflict in Iran, which has driven up fuel prices. DeSantis said some Republicans have tried to blame former President Joe Biden for the higher prices, but he urged them to be honest. LIVE RESULTS: Florida Senate midterm election "Gas is higher and it hurts people, working-class people," he said. "And it's higher because of this conflict. That's just a fact. If you can't admit that to voters, then you're gaslighting them and they're not going to listen to you on other things." DeSantis unsuccessfully competed with Trump for the 2024 presidential nomination and could run again in 2028. Sen. Susan Collins tries to keep her seat while fending off Troy Jackson Collins is running for her sixth term on a pledge to continue serving Maine as one of the few remaining moderates in the Senate. The Republican faces a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson, who entered the race late. Jackson has tried to paint Collins as too close to Trump, while Collins has touted her willingness to break from the rest of the Republican Party on key votes. Collins is the only Republican senator from New England, and she has triumphed in previous tough elections. This time, Democrats focused on unseating her from the beginning, but the party's June primary winner, Graham Platner, withdrew from the race after facing sexual assault allegations that he denied. Jackson became the new nominee after winning a special nominating convention in late July. Justice Department dispatches 1,000 election monitors to the polls The Justice Department announced early Tuesday that it is sending roughly 1,000 federal election monitors to all 50 states to observe Election Day voting. Many are expected in populated areas that tend to vote for Democrats. They include past hot spots for election tensions, like Detroit, Philadelphia and Georgia's Fulton County. The monitoring program isn't new, but it has faced criticism from voting rights groups concerned about federal interference and voter intimidation. The NAACP sued after the department said it would include law enforcement officers in the program, but a judge ruled against the group overnight, arguing the government had made it clear that monitors would be in plainclothes, would not carry firearms and wouldn't have the power to make arrests at poll sites. The Justice Department has said its monitors will observe and will not interfere with voting. House races playing out deep in Trump country People leave a polling station at a town hall during the midterm elections, in Bramwell, West Virginia, on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Marcus Constantino/ Reuters A campaign sign for Democratic Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa near a polling station during the US midterm elections, on Election Day, in Austin, Texas, US, November 3, 2026. REUTERS/Mike Segar Republicans are mostly on defense in the battle for control of the U.S. House. Most of the top battlegrounds are districts Trump won in 2024, sometimes by a lot. Republicans and allied groups pulled spending from several House races in October, shifting, for example, away from GOP incumbents in Iowa and New Jersey. At Trump's urging, Republicans in states including Texas and Florida tried to give themselves a boost with early redistricting, but that may turn out to be a flop. Democrats are defending a handful of seats in Trump country as well, and there are pockets of potential GOP upside around the country. The AP has a detailed rundown of the House districts in play and the fight for the majority. Senate control up for grabs in states Trump carried Control of the Senate hangs in the balance in a way few could have foreseen. Originally, Democrats believed they only had a narrow path to the majority, and their plan required flipping seats in Alaska, Ohio, Maine and North Carolina. However, the map has shifted, and Democrats believe they have a shot at Texas, Kansas and Iowa as well. READ MORE: 13 races that will determine control of the Senate Many of these are states Trump won by double-digit margins two years ago. Democrats need to play defense as well. Although they're expected to hold Georgia, they also need to lock down Michigan and Minnesota. In Maine, a voter feels 'the weight of the world' In Falmouth, Maine, 60-year-old Susan Myers said she's optimistic that Senate candidate Troy Jackson can take advantage of anti-Trump sentiment and defeat longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins. She's also aware of how recent elections have gone for diehard Democrats like herself. "I'm hopeful. I feel like there's been so much disappointment these last few election cycles that I don't want to get my hopes up," she said. LIVE RESULTS: Maine Senate midterm election Myers voted early at Falmouth Town Hall and was picking up an absentee ballot for her daughter. She said so much national attention on Maine this election has been overwhelming. The Senate race is one of this year's most competitive and could decide which party controls the chamber. "It feels a little bit like we have the weight of the world on our shoulders," Myers said. Latinos form a crucial bloc of swing voters Latinos helped return Trump to the White House in 2024. Now they're poised to play an outsized role in the midterms. The path to a U.S. House majority runs through heavily Latino districts in states such as Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida and Texas. The front-line Senate race in Texas likewise could hinge on Latinos. WATCH: GOP's big bet on Texas Latino voters could backfire in midterms About 6 in 10 Hispanic adults disapprove of Trump's handling of the presidency, according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll from October. About 7 in 10 disapprove of his performance on the economy. One key factor will be how effective Democrats have been at making the case for themselves. Will disaffected Trump supporters vote for Democrats, or just sit out the midterms? In Michigan's Senate race, history and control of the chamber are on the line Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is seeking to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. Republican Mike Rogers wants to be the first member of his party to win a Michigan Senate race in more than three decades. The contest to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is among a handful that could determine which party controls the Senate. Although Michigan Democrats have been successful in recent midterm elections, Trump carried the battleground state in two of his three campaigns. That divided political landscape helped set the stage for one of the most bitter and contentious Senate races of the cycle. El-Sayed has accused Rogers of being a "puppet" for Trump. Rogers has accused El-Sayed of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, while Trump has falsely called the Democrat a "jihadist." Progressives are hoping an El-Sayed victory will signal their agenda can resonate in a battleground state ahead of the next presidential election. Millions of Americans will be voting in new congressional districts Mid-decade redistricting shook up the House map ahead of the midterms, changing the boundaries of around one-third of congressional districts. The AP analyzed each district's 2024 presidential vote margin before and after redistricting and found that while many individual districts saw dramatic shifts in partisanship and demographic makeup, the national U.S. House map did not shift significantly toward either party. Learn more about how redistricting shaped the 2026 midterm elections and see how your district boundaries changed in this map. Midterm results will chart the course of Trump's final two years Trump is staring down twin threats from Capitol Hill for his last two years as president if his party loses at least one chamber in Tuesday's midterms: investigations and impeachment. Democratic lawmakers are eager to exercise oversight, with senior officials long telegraphing how they would go after an administration they believe has escaped accountability for policies, personal profits and abuses of power. The majority party controls gavels on powerful House committees, which come with larger staff budgets and more expansive resources, including subpoena powers. Less certain are prospects for impeaching Trump, although House Democratic leaders will almost certainly come under pressure from their left flank to do so. Rather than Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term but acquitted by the Senate both times, Democrats may instead try to impeach Cabinet officials. If Republicans lose the Senate, Trump's ability to push his judicial and executive branch nominees through to confirmation will also be severely weakened. Races for Senate, governor in Iowa are open for the first time since 1968 Iowa's top of the ticket is up for grabs after Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds and Sen. Joni Ernst opted out of reelection bids. Republicans control state government and comprise the entirety of Iowa's federal delegation. But the openings have given Democrats opportunities to win over voters who may want a new direction amid high grocery and gas prices, manufacturing job losses, a crippled agricultural economy and growing cancer rates. In the governor's race, Rob Sand, the state auditor and only Democrat in statewide elected office, faces Republican Zach Lahn, a political newcomer who stunned even members of his own party when he won the primary over a Trump-endorsed congressman. Democrat Josh Turek and Republican Ashley Hinson are competing for a U.S. Senate seat. Hinson, a congresswoman endorsed by Trump, has tried to assure voters she will push back when his policies are wrong for Iowa. Turek, a state lawmaker, was endorsed by Barack Obama, the last Democrat seeking federal office to win Iowa before Trump won the last three presidential elections. Judge blocks Trump administration from sending lists of alleged noncitizen voters A federal judge has ruled that the Trump administration must stop sending voter lists of alleged noncitizens to election officials, as it has done in California and Washington state, while urging the states to set aside those ballots. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan in Washington, D.C., said in her decision late Monday that more voter data transmissions would likely confuse voters and election officials at a time when election resources need to be focused on administering the midterms. States and voting rights groups have pushed back on the administration's claims and said the lists are riddled with errors. The decision is one in a string of court losses for the administration in its efforts to expand federal authority over elections, which are run by the states. Southwest flooding forces the Navajo Nation to change some Election Day voting plans The Navajo Election Administration says it has altered five polling locations — two in Arizona and three in New Mexico. The tribe's reservation surrounds the Four Corners Monument, where Arizona, New Mexico, Utah and Colorado meet. The area has seen major flooding since October, with rivers overflowing their banks and some residents having to evacuate. The tribe says it has more than 298,000 members. GOP loses immigration advantage Trump roared back to power due to the Biden administration's border troubles. He cut illegal crossings of the border, which were already plummeting, to close to zero. That's when the trouble started. The president turned to the trickier task of deporting people in the U.S. illegally from the interior. Soon the main image of illegal immigration wasn't desperate people crossing the border, but mothers screaming as they were torn from their children, or masked federal agents chasing people — sometimes citizens — through streets. Trump openly bemoaned how the U.S. didn't get enough migrants from Scandinavian countries and only accepted white South Africans into the country as refugees. And then two citizen protesters were shot and killed by immigration agents during the administration's raids on Minneapolis. Now the GOP fears it will especially lose ground in immigrant-rich areas running from New Jersey to Florida to Texas. And polls show more voters oppose Trump on immigration than support him. Democrats are hopeful — but not optimistic — in South Carolina Lindsey Graham's sudden death left South Carolina Republicans scrambling to pick a new nominee in a special primary, which his sister, Darline Graham, ultimately won. The switch-up left the state's Democrats with renewed hope they could break a 20-year drought on winning a statewide race. But even some of Democratic nominee Annie Andrews' supporters acknowledge their state might not yet be ready to go blue, despite Democrats' advances in neighboring North Carolina and Georgia. South Carolina has consistently backed Trump, who endorsed Graham, urged her to run and has stumped twice for her in the state. Graham and Andrews have portrayed each other as ill-prepared for the role. Latest views on Trump from AP-NORC polling Trump might not be on the ballot, but Americans are very unhappy with his performance so far in his second term. Only about one-third of U.S. adults, 35%, approve of how Trump is handling the presidency, according to AP-NORC polling from October. Trump's approval tends to stay within a fairly narrow range, but the most recent measure is below where his overall approval stood shortly after he started his second term, when 42% of U.S. adults approved of how he was handling the presidency. He's seen modest declines in approval among Republicans and independents. About 70% of Republicans approve of how Trump is handling the presidency, down from 82% at the start of his term. Trump's current approval rating is slightly below where it stood in October 2018. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Polls close in first states as voters decide control of Congress
(Updates with polls beginning to close)
DETROIT >> The first polls closed today after millions of Americans voted in midterm elections that could strip President Donald Trump’s Republicans of control of Congress, with Democrats favored in opinion polls to capture the House and a handful of Senate races set to determine whether they can seize both chambers.
The battle for the Senate is unfolding across nearly 10 closely contested statewide races, most in Republican strongholds.
Polling stations began to close in Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. ET (1 p.m. Hawaii time) and will close in another half-dozen states at 7 p.m., but remain open for hours yet in most states.
>> RELATED: Hawaii election officials urge putting ballots in drop boxes today
History is against Trump’s Republicans: The sitting president’s party has lost ground in Congress in all but two midterms since World War Two. Trump’s approval rating is hovering near his career lows, with voters frustrated by war with Iran, higher fuel prices and wider affordability concerns.
Don't miss out on what's happening!
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
There is little doubt this year’s election is all about Trump, nearly halfway through his second four-year term. Trump himself has told his supporters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” a message Democratic leaders have happily echoed.
>> RELATED: Few charges emerge from Trump campaign against noncitizen voters
In televised remarks today that appeared aimed at swaying voters unhappy with U.S. support for Israel, Trump said that he intended to stop $3.8 billion in promised annual funding to Israel after the end of this year, but it was unclear how he would do so, given a 2020 law mandating the funding levels.
The close U.S.-Israel alliance has been a particular focus in Michigan, where progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim U.S. senator if elected, has faced millions of dollars in opposition spending from Israel-linked groups over his criticisms of the U.S. ally.
El-Sayed, 42, posed for photos with voters in sunglasses and a signature tight black T-shirt at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor today. Led by Trump, Republicans have portrayed El-Sayed and other Democratic candidates as radical, un-American and even communist, labels that Democrats dismiss as typical Trump hyperbole.
The president has sought to energize his base with more than two dozen campaign rallies since the start of October, most in states he easily won in 2024.
Opinion polls show voters are most concerned about affordability and disapprove of Trump’s handling of the issue. His tariffs on imports, many of which were thrown out by the courts, and his decision to attack Iran in February raised prices for consumers.
At a voting center in a predominantly Black neighborhood in Detroit, Natalia Towns, 34, said she did not find efforts by Mike Rogers, 63, the Republican Senate candidate, to court Black voters sincere. Towns felt El-Sayed would do more to bring down costs.
“I do feel like health matters, gas prices are high, food is too high,” she said.
At a polling station in the predominantly white suburb of Warren, to Detroit’s north, Paul Stockyj said he voted for Rogers, describing El-Sayed as too progressive.
“I would not like to see somebody be that ambitious to tackle all the problems,” Stockyj said. “Who’s going to pay for all the stuff that he wants to do? People that are going to pay for it are you and me.”
Problems with machines that scan paper ballots were reported in various parts of the country, including counties in Georgia, Iowa, Mississippi and New York, slowing down voting and ballot-counting.
Isolated voting machine malfunctions are not unusual for U.S. elections, but election experts say that backup systems and other safeguards mean these rarely affect results.
Legal observers and Democrats have warned that Trump, who has long falsely claimed that U.S. elections are rigged, may attempt to challenge today’s results if Republicans lose.
The Justice Department said it had deployed 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states in what it called the largest Election Day monitoring effort in history.
Democrats criticized the plan as potential voter intimidation. In roughly two-thirds of the jurisdictions the department listed, voters supported Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump in the 2024 presidential election, a Reuters analysis found.
All 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are up for election, along with 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats, though most contests are not considered competitive. Democrats must flip at least three House seats and four Senate seats to win a majority in each chamber.
Democrats have little margin for error in the Senate. The party must defend all of its current seats while winning at least two states that voted for Trump by a double-digit margin two years ago: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas.
Opinion polls show Democrats either narrowly leading or within striking distance in all of those states.
The Alaska Senate race has been thrown into turmoil after the New York Times reported that the campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, 53, helped recruit a third candidate to run as an independent who shares the first and last name of her Republican opponent, Dan Sullivan, 61.
>> RELATED: DOJ sends target letters to 20 Democrats in Alaska election inquiry
Peltola has denied involvement. Trump’s Justice Department has launched a criminal probe into the
Peltola has denied involvement. Trump’s Justice Department has launched a criminal probe into the allegations and filed a lawsuit to block certification of the election results, though a judge dismissed the latter effort.
The Justice Department is notifying more than 20 people they are subjects of the criminal probe, according to a person familiar with the investigation who spoke on the condition of anonymity to talk about the investigation.
Since the Times story, Trump has repeatedly complained that many Americans do not know what ‘incumbent’ means. But supporters of the incumbent Sullivan told Reuters they were familiar with the word, and they were not confused by the two Dan Sullivans on their ballot.
“They make it pretty obvious: it says ‘incumbent’ after his name,” said Jake Wesley, 27, who grew up in Anchorage and is now stationed there in the U.S. Air Force.
In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, 37, has his party once again dreaming of winning the Republican-favoring state after decades of heartbreak. His scandal-plagued opponent, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, 63, has benefited from hundreds of millions of dollars donated on his behalf by Elon Musk.
There are 47 U.S. House races widely seen as competitive, according to a Reuters analysis of the leading election forecasters. If the other contests all proceed as predicted, Democrats would need to win only 13 of those races to secure a majority.
Additional reporting by Dan Catchpole, Ashraf Fahim, Arafat Barbakh, David Morgan, Mike Spector, Bianca Flowers, Pete Eisler, Doina Chiacu and Humeyra Pamuk.
