Poll closing times: when polls close in 10 U.S. states
sources.text:
Why election results arrive in waves: poll closing times in 10 U.S. states
These poll closing times for 10 U.S. states show what time polls close on election night, how time zones split some states and why results arrive in waves
Election results in the U.S. arrive in waves, not all at once. Two facts explain that pattern. Each state decides when its polls close, and the country stretches across six time zones. The first polls close at 6 p.m. Eastern in parts of Indiana and Kentucky. Voting on the West Coast, and in Alaska and Hawaii, continues for hours after that.
Federal general elections take place on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November. The date is the same nationwide, but the hours are not. State law sets voting hours. That means the answer to "what time do polls close" depends on where a voter lives.
Every closing time is set in local time. That detail matters most in states that straddle two time zones. The clock reads the same hour at closing in both regions, but the moments are an hour apart. In effect, such a state has two closing moments on election night. Polls in the more westerly zone stay open an hour longer in real time.
Closing time does not always end voting. Most states let people who are already in line when polls close remain and cast a ballot. The details differ by state. Voters should check their own state's rule before election day.
Hours can also change. Closing times are fixed by state law, and legislatures can revise them between elections. A time that applied in one cycle may not apply in the next. Voters should confirm their hours with their state or county election office.
This guide covers poll closing times in 10 U.S. states and state groups. It is a selection, not a full 50-state list. The entries run roughly from the earliest closings to later ones, measured in Eastern time, and end with Alaska and Hawaii. Each entry gives the closing hour and the time zone it applies to. Several show how a split time zone creates a second closing moment inside one state. The West Coast entry explains why results there come in after much of the country has finished voting.
Indiana and Kentucky polls close at 6 p.m. local time
Illustration: Quartz
Indiana and Kentucky close their polls at 6 p.m. local time, the earliest closing time in the country by the local clock. Both states span the Eastern and Central time zones.
Most of Indiana and most of Kentucky sit in the Eastern time zone. In those areas, voting ends at 6 p.m. Eastern. That zone includes the largest cities in both states, among them Indianapolis, Louisville and Lexington.
The western portions of each state run on Central time. Polls there also close at 6 p.m., but by the local clock. In Eastern terms, that is 7 p.m. — an hour after the Eastern-zone precincts in the same state have stopped voting.
In Indiana, the Central-time areas sit in two corners of the state. One is the northwest, near Chicago, which includes Gary. The other is the southwest, around Evansville. In Kentucky, the Central zone covers the western part of the state. Bowling Green, Owensboro and Paducah all fall on that side of the line.
The split matters for anyone following returns. A precinct in eastern Kentucky can finish voting while polls in Paducah stay open for another hour. The same gap separates Indianapolis from Evansville. Early returns from either state come only from areas where voting has already ended.
Polls in both states open at 6 a.m. local time. That gives voters a 12-hour window on election day. States that close at 7 p.m. or later leave more time after work. Voters who usually cast ballots in the evening should plan around the earlier finish.
Most states let voters who are in line at closing time cast a ballot, but the specifics vary by state. Voters in Indiana and Kentucky should check their own state's rule rather than count on it.
Indiana and Kentucky set these hours by state law, and either legislature can revise them. The Indiana Election Division and the Kentucky State Board of Elections, along with county election officials, publish current hours and polling locations.
Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia polls close at 7 p.m. Eastern
Illustration: Quartz
Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia all close their polls at 7 p.m. Eastern time. All three states sit entirely within the Eastern time zone. Each therefore has a single closing moment that covers the whole state.
No part of any of the three states keeps voting an hour longer than the rest. That sets them apart from neighbors divided by a time-zone line. A precinct on the Georgia coast and one in the north Georgia mountains close at the same instant.
The three states differ on when voting begins. Georgia and South Carolina open their polls at 7 a.m., giving voters a 12-hour window. Virginia opens at 6 a.m., which stretches its voting day to 13 hours.
Election watchers elsewhere in the U.S. see this deadline at an earlier local hour. The 7 p.m. Eastern closing arrives at 6 p.m. Central, 5 p.m. Mountain and 4 p.m. Pacific.
By 7 p.m. Eastern, voting has ended across all of Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia. Indiana and Kentucky finish statewide at that moment too, as their Central-time polls close an hour after the Eastern parts of those states. The Eastern-time portion of Florida, which covers most of the state, also closes then. Polls in the western Panhandle stay open another hour.
Closing time is not always the last moment to vote. Voters already in line at 7 p.m. should check how their state treats them. Those rules are not identical everywhere.
Poll hours in all three states come from state law, which legislatures can amend between elections. Each state's election office posts the current hours. In Georgia, that is the Secretary of State's office. In Virginia, it is the Department of Elections. County election offices post hours too. Virginia's independent cities have their own election offices, separate from the counties. A quick check before heading out confirms the deadline that applies.
Florida poll closing times in Eastern and Central time zones
Illustration: Quartz
Florida polls close at 7 p.m. local time on election day. For most of the state that means 7 p.m. Eastern, while the western Panhandle closes at 7 p.m. Central, or 8 p.m. Eastern.
Florida's polls also open at 7 a.m. local time. That gives every precinct a 12-hour voting day, whichever zone it sits in. In the Central-time Panhandle, the first ballots go in at 8 a.m. Eastern.
The peninsula and most of northern Florida sit in the Eastern zone. The western end of the Panhandle sits in the Central zone. For much of its length, the Apalachicola River marks the line between the two.
Tallahassee, the state capital, keeps Eastern time. Pensacola, near the Alabama line, keeps Central time, as do Panama City and Fort Walton Beach. Voters in all four cities follow the same 7 p.m. rule. Polls in Tallahassee still close an hour before the others.
That gap shows up on election night. Once 7 p.m. Eastern passes, most Florida precincts have closed. Polling places in the Central-time Panhandle stay open for one more hour.
For a Panhandle voter, the local clock is the one that counts. A Central-time polling place closes at 7 p.m. as shown on a phone set to local time. The Eastern conversion matters mostly to people following results from elsewhere in the country.
Most states let those already waiting at closing cast a ballot. Voters who arrive close to 7 p.m. should check how their county handles people still in line at closing.
Each of Florida's 67 counties has its own supervisor of elections. That office handles polling places and precinct assignments for its county. The Florida Division of Elections, part of the Florida Department of State, oversees elections statewide. Either office can confirm the hours in force for an upcoming election. State law sets those hours, and lawmakers can revise them.
Ohio, North Carolina and West Virginia close polls at 7:30 p.m. Eastern
Illustration: Quartz
Polls in Ohio, North Carolina and West Virginia close at 7:30 p.m. Eastern time. The three states share a half-hour closing slot between the 7 p.m. and 8 p.m. Eastern closings.
On the Eastern clock, that slot sits in the middle of the early evening sequence. Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia close 30 minutes earlier, at 7 p.m. Eastern. Most of Florida closes at the same hour.
A few split-zone areas also finish ahead of these three states. The Central-time portions of Indiana and Kentucky close at 6 p.m. local time, which is 7 p.m. Eastern. The Eastern-zone parts of those two states close 90 minutes before Ohio, North Carolina and West Virginia.
The next group of closings comes 30 minutes after the 7:30 p.m. slot. Pennsylvania and most of Michigan close at 8 p.m. Eastern. Florida's western Panhandle closes at the same moment. Its polls shut at 7 p.m. Central, which equals 8 p.m. Eastern.
Most of Texas also closes at that moment. The state's Central-time polls shut at 7 p.m. Central, or 8 p.m. Eastern.
Later closings continue for hours. New York closes at 9 p.m. Eastern, 90 minutes after these three states. Michigan's Central-time counties in the western Upper Peninsula close at 8 p.m. Central, which is also 9 p.m. Eastern.
For readers outside the Eastern zone, a 7:30 p.m. Eastern closing equals 6:30 p.m. Central, 5:30 p.m. Mountain and 4:30 p.m. Pacific. California, Oregon and Washington state close at 8 p.m. Pacific, or 11 p.m. Eastern. That leaves three and a half hours between the 7:30 p.m. Eastern deadline and the West Coast close.
Hawaii and Alaska close on their own local clocks. Hawaii closes at 7 p.m. Hawaii Standard Time, and Alaska closes at 8 p.m. Alaska Standard Time.
The 7:30 p.m. hour is a legal setting, not a fixed tradition. Voters in Ohio, North Carolina and West Virginia can check the current hour, along with their polling place, with local election officials ahead of election day.
Pennsylvania polls close at 8 p.m. Eastern
Illustration: Quartz
Pennsylvania polls close at 8 p.m. Eastern time on election day. The whole state sits in the Eastern time zone. One closing moment applies everywhere from Philadelphia to Pittsburgh to Erie.
A voter in any county faces the same cutoff. There is no second local closing time to track. That sets Pennsylvania apart from split-zone states such as Florida, Texas and Michigan.
Two of Pennsylvania's neighbors finish voting earlier. Ohio and West Virginia, which border the state to the west and south, close their polls at 7:30 p.m. Eastern. Pennsylvania voters get another 30 minutes. New York, along the northern border, closes at 9 p.m. Eastern. That is an hour after Pennsylvania.
Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia close even earlier, at 7 p.m. Eastern. Their polls shut an hour before Pennsylvania's. In the Central-time parts of Indiana and Kentucky, polls close at 7 p.m. Eastern, also an hour before Pennsylvania.
The 8 p.m. Eastern slot is not Pennsylvania's alone. Most of Michigan closes at the same hour. Florida's western Panhandle runs on Central time and closes at 7 p.m. Central. That is the same moment Pennsylvania's polls shut. Most of Texas, which runs on Central time, closes at 7 p.m. Central. That also lands at 8 p.m. Eastern. The result is a cluster of closings at a single instant across several states.
On the West Coast, clocks read 5 p.m. when Pennsylvania's deadline passes. California, Oregon and Washington state close at 8 p.m. Pacific, which is 11 p.m. Eastern. Voting there continues for three hours after Pennsylvania's polls close.
Voters still in line at 8 p.m. may fall under the in-line rule that most states follow. The Pennsylvania Department of State can explain how that rule applies in Pennsylvania.
State law sets Pennsylvania's poll hours, and lawmakers can revise them between elections. A county board of elections can confirm the current schedule before a voter heads to the polls.
Texas polls close at 7 p.m., with El Paso on Mountain time
Illustration: Quartz
Texas polls close at 7 p.m. local time on election day. Most of the state follows Central time. El Paso and the far western corner follow Mountain time, where polls close at 7 p.m. Mountain, or 8 p.m. Central.
The time-zone line means voting in Texas ends in two stages. The first comes at 7 p.m. Central, when polls shut across the bulk of the state. The second arrives an hour later on the Central clock, when El Paso and the surrounding far west reach their own 7 p.m. deadline.
Readers who follow election night on Eastern time need one more conversion. A 7 p.m. Central closing is 8 p.m. Eastern. A 7 p.m. Mountain closing is 9 p.m. Eastern. Texas finishes voting across two separate hours of the national evening, not one.
Those two moments line up with other states' closings. The Central-zone close in Texas lands at the same moment as Pennsylvania's 8 p.m. Eastern deadline. The El Paso close matches New York's 9 p.m. Eastern closing.
A voter standing in either zone faces a single deadline. Polls close at 7 p.m. on whatever clock the polling place follows. A voter in El Paso does not need to convert anything. The Mountain-time deadline applies there, and it reads 7 p.m., just as it does in Dallas or Houston.
The split matters more for people outside the polling place. Campaign staff, newsrooms and viewers in other zones need to know that voting has not ended everywhere in Texas at the first closing. In El Paso and the far west, ballots are still being cast for another hour.
Texas shares this kind of split with several other states. Elsewhere, the line runs through a panhandle, a peninsula or a cluster of western counties. In Texas, it separates El Paso and the far west from everything to the east.
Voting hours in Texas come from state law, which legislators can amend. Before heading to the polls, Texas voters can check current hours with their county elections office.
Michigan polls close at 8 p.m., including Upper Peninsula Central-time counties
Illustration: Quartz
Michigan polls close at 8 p.m. local time on election day. Most of the state closes at 8 p.m. Eastern, while Central-time counties in the western Upper Peninsula close at 8 p.m. Central, which is 9 p.m. Eastern.
Polls across Michigan open at 7 a.m. local time. The opening hour follows the same pattern as the closing hour. A polling place on Central time opens an hour later in real terms than one in Detroit, and it closes an hour later too.
Eastern time covers the entire Lower Peninsula and most of the Upper Peninsula. The Lower Peninsula holds the large majority of Michigan's residents. As a result, the 8 p.m. Eastern deadline applies to most of the state's voters.
The Central-time counties sit at the far western end of the Upper Peninsula, along the border with Wisconsin. Wisconsin keeps Central time as well. These communities share a clock with their neighbors across the state line rather than with Lansing, the state capital.
That geography means a voter in Detroit and a voter near the Wisconsin line both face an 8 p.m. deadline. Their deadlines fall an hour apart. Voting in Michigan is not finished statewide until 9 p.m. Eastern, even though most of the state stops admitting new voters an hour before that.
For an individual voter, the deadline that counts is 8 p.m. on the local clock at the assigned polling place. Someone who lives in one zone and works in the other should plan around the time where they vote, not where they spend the workday.
Questions about voters still in line at 8 p.m. are best directed to local election officials.
Elections in Michigan are run largely by city and township clerks, not only by county offices. The clerk who oversees a voter's polling place can confirm the current hours, as can the Michigan Secretary of State. Polling hours are written into state law, so checking before election day protects against relying on an older schedule.
New York polls close at 9 p.m. Eastern
Illustration: Quartz
New York polls close at 9 p.m. Eastern time on election day. That puts the state among the later closing times in the contiguous U.S., three hours after the first polls shut in Indiana and Kentucky.
The whole state lies in the Eastern time zone. Every polling place, from Buffalo to Long Island, closes at the same moment. Voters and election watchers have a single closing time to track.
Polls in New York open at 6 a.m. on general election day. Combined with the 9 p.m. close, that gives in-person voters a 15-hour voting window.
New York also offers in-person early voting in the days before election day. Early voting sites keep separate hours set by county boards. The 9 p.m. close applies to election day itself.
In Eastern terms, New York's close comes an hour after Pennsylvania's polls shut at 8 p.m. Eastern. It also lines up with closings in two other zones. Michigan's Upper Peninsula counties on Central time close at 8 p.m. Central, which is 9 p.m. Eastern. Far west Texas, on Mountain time, closes at 7 p.m. Mountain. That is also 9 p.m. Eastern.
When New York's polls close, clocks on the West Coast read 6 p.m. Voters in California, Oregon and Washington state still have two more hours. Polls there close at 8 p.m. Pacific, or 11 p.m. Eastern.
Most states let people already in line at closing time cast a ballot. Late arrivals in New York should confirm how that works locally rather than assume it applies.
County boards of elections run voting across New York. The New York City Board of Elections handles the five boroughs. These offices and the New York State Board of Elections publish polling hours and locations before each election. Closing times are set in state law and can change. A check with the local board before election day confirms when a given polling place shuts.
California, Oregon and Washington state polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific
Illustration: Quartz
California, Oregon and Washington state close their polls at 8 p.m. Pacific time. On the East Coast, that moment arrives at 11 p.m. Eastern. The timing places the three West Coast states among the final closings of election night in the contiguous U.S.
The three-hour gap shapes the rhythm of a national election night. By the time West Coast polls shut, voting has already ended across much of the rest of the country. Viewers on the East Coast may have followed returns from other regions for hours before the first West Coast results appear.
For voters in Los Angeles, Portland or Seattle, the deadline reads 8 p.m. on the local clock. Pennsylvania voters see that same hour on their own clocks. The difference lies in the time zone, not the hour.
The November general election always falls after daylight saving time ends on the first Sunday of that month. As a result, the West Coast deadline runs on Pacific Standard Time.
Pacific time covers nearly all of the territory in the three states, but Oregon has an exception. Most of Malheur County, in the eastern part of the state, observes Mountain time. Voters there should confirm the exact local deadline with the county elections office.
Oregon and Washington state conduct their elections primarily by mail. In those two states, the 8 p.m. Pacific cutoff applies mainly to official ballot drop boxes and in-person voting centers. Ballots sent through the postal system may follow separate rules. Voters should check those rules with their county before relying on the mail.
California voters who choose an in-person location on election day face the same 8 p.m. Pacific deadline. As in most states, people already standing in line at closing time can generally still vote, though each state writes its own rules.
Legislatures set these hours in state law and can revise them between elections. The state or county elections office in California, Oregon or Washington state is the place to confirm the current time before setting out to vote.
Hawaii and Alaska poll closing times in their own time zones
Illustration: Quartz
Hawaii polls close at 7 p.m. Hawaii Standard Time. Alaska polls close at 8 p.m. Alaska Standard Time.
Each hour belongs to its own clock. Hawaii's 7 p.m. and Alaska's 8 p.m. are not readings from one shared zone. A higher number on the local clock does not, by itself, show which state stops voting later in real time. Neither hour is stated in Pacific or Eastern time. Lining the two up would require converting both to a single zone.
Both states lie outside the contiguous U.S. Each runs on a time zone that no mainland state uses. This entry treats them together for that reason, rather than folding them into the West Coast group. The pairing reflects geography and clocks, not a shared closing hour.
For a voter, the local clock is the one that counts. Someone casting a ballot in Honolulu should go by Hawaii time. Someone voting in Anchorage should go by Alaska time. A phone set to another zone, or a travel plan written in mainland time, can point to the wrong hour.
National coverage adds another layer. A broadcast schedule built around Eastern time may list these closings in a different zone. The times on screen then will not match the clock at a Honolulu or Anchorage polling place. The local hour is the one that governs when voting ends.
Each closing time is set by state law, and lawmakers can revise it. Hawaii voters can confirm current hours with the state Office of Elections or their county clerk. Alaska voters can check with the state Division of Elections. A check close to election day avoids relying on an outdated hour.
Anyone still waiting to vote at closing time should ask a poll worker how the cutoff applies at that location.

sources.news_title: How the midterms shape the last two years of a presidency
Trump faces crucial test amid low ratings, Democrats aim to flip Senate as US votes in midterm polls
US midterms: Trump risks losing grip on Congress as Americans vote
sources.text:
Washington: Americans began voting on Tuesday, November 2, in one of the most consequential elections in recent times, widely seen as a referendum on Donald Trump‘s presidency that has been marked by a prolonged war in Iran, rising inflation, trade wars and deep divisions in society.
The polling will decide whether President Trump’s Republican Party retains control of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers of the US Congress, or, as opinion polls are predicting, the Democratic Party wrests control of at least the House if not the Senate, also in the final two years of Trump’s second term in office.
On the eve of the elections, the US launched limited strikes on Iran’s Qesham island in the Hormuz Strait. Officials said that the strikes were in response to Iran firing at a US aircraft.
At stake in the elections are all 435 seats of the House and 37 seats in the 100-member Senate.
In Ohio, Indian American Vivek Ramaswamy contests Amy Acton
Elections are also being held for the post of Governor in 36 states, including in Ohio, where Indian American Vivek Ramaswamy is locked in a keen contest with his rival and Democratic nominee Amy Acton.
A number of Indian American candidates are in the electoral fray for posts ranging from Governor to city council members. Democrat Nithya Raman, who was born in Kerala, is locked in a keen contest with her former boss Karen Bass for the post of Mayor of Los Angeles, the second-largest city in the US.
Indian-American lawmakers Ro Khanna, Ami Bera, Pramila Jayapal and Suhas Subramanyam are seeking re-election to the US House of Representatives, while fellow Democrats Pia Dandiya and Amish Shah are in the fray in competitive races to make their debut as Congresspersons.
Trump’s whirlwind tour of 20 states in 32 days
On Monday, the Republicans and the Democrats made their final pitch to the voters, with Trump choosing an unusual venue – the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool – to focus on the renovations undertaken in the national capital instead of talking about tax cuts, tariffs and border security, which have been the high points of his election rallies.
According to the White House, Trump did a whirlwind tour of 20 states, mostly Republican strongholds, to address 30 rallies in the last 32 days. Analysts say his approval ratings are at an all-time low, and he has become a liability to Republican candidates.
If the pre-poll forecasts come true and Democrats take control of the US Congress, it will allow for deeper Congressional scrutiny and checks of Trump’s actions, which will severely limit his ability to push his agenda. He will, however, retain the power to govern through executive orders, which will be valid for two years.
I guess I’ll become Mr Veto: Trump
“We are reaching a boiling point in the country as a whole. There are the elites, the ruling class, the Epstein class that is truly 1 per cent that is wealthy, and there is the rest of us,” Shuchita Patel, a Democrat, who is running for the post of Forsyth County Commissioner, told PTI.
Trump acknowledged the possibility of his wings being clipped but indicated that he will not allow Congress to slow him down.
“I guess I’ll become Mr Veto,” Trump told the New York Post’s Pod Force One podcast in response to a question on Republicans losing control of both Houses of the US Congress, referring to the presidential power to veto actions by Congress.
Obama urges voters to ‘flip’ the circuit breaker election
Former President Barack Obama boosted the Democratic campaign with rallies in Ohio, Michigan and Georgia, which clearly left Trump rattled.
“This election is our last, best chance of at least reining him in, reining in some of the foolishness of this administration,” Obama said in Georgia.
“It’s the circuit-breaker in the system, and we need to flip it,” he said, taking Trump to task for focusing on White House renovations instead of issues affecting the people.
Democrats rally behind El-Sayed despite setback
The upbeat Democrats, however, suffered an unexpected setback in the eleventh hour when Congresswoman Haley Stevens of Michigan crossed over to the Republican side on Sunday, breaking ranks with Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who could be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
The Democratic Party quickly rallied behind El-Sayed by issuing statements condemning Stevens, who sprung a surprise by endorsing El-Sayed’s Republican rival, Mike Rogers, and appearing alongside him in public.
Stevens lost in the Senate primary to El-Sayed. She is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the US ally.
The Democrats are hoping to flip seven Senate seats — Michigan, Maine, Ohio, Kansas, Texas, Iowa and Alaska — in their bid to gain a majority in the 100-member House.
US Congress system
Each of the 50 states in the United States is represented by two Senators who sit in the Congress for a six-year term. But the Senators are divided into three lots, and their terms are staggered so that elections are held every two years.
The House members are elected for a two-year term.
Republicans enjoy a majority in both chambers of Congress, but by thin margins.
In the House of Representatives, Speaker Mike Johnson has 218 Republicans and one independent, Kevin Kiley of California, against 214 Democrats, with two seats vacant.
The Senate is split 53-47 in favour of the Republicans. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to wrest control of the chamber. Of the 35 Senate seats are on the ballot, 22 are held by Republicans.
Why midterms are crucial for Vance
The mid-term elections are also crucial for Vice President JD Vance, who is burnishing his credentials to become a successor to Trump’s mantle.
Vance made campaign stops in New York and Ohio on Monday, where Republicans were fighting for House and Senate seats.
He highlighted Trump’s moves to end taxes on tips and overtime and secure the border while branding Democrats as “lunatics” who have contempt for American voters.
About 210 million Americans are registered to vote, according to USAFacts. California has the most registered voters, with 23.2 million, followed by Texas (17.4 million) and Florida (13.6 million). Together, they account for about 26 per cent of all registered voters.
Wyoming (278,468), Vermont (459,455) and Alaska (603,310) have the fewest.
According to the AP, more than 57 million ballots have been cast in 47 states and D.C. as of Monday, compared to a little under 44.5 million in 49 states and D.C. in 2022.

sources.news_title: The Latest: Voters will decide control of Congress in major test of Trump's second term
sources.text:
Voters across the country are deciding control of the U.S. House and Senate in the 2026 midterm elections. Democrats must flip four seats in the Senate and three seats in the House to wrest control of the chambers from Republicans. Polls have closed in 11 states, and results are beginning to roll into AP’s election system. Here’s when we can expect more results throughout the night.
Power in Congress would give Democrats a means of rebuffing President Donald Trump’s agenda during the final two years of his term. The battle for control is playing out mostly in states and districts Trump previously won by wide margins. All eyes are on Senate contests in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas. House battlegrounds are scattered across the country.
Recommended Videos
Voters say the economy and the state of democracy are the top issues facing the country, with high costs and government corruption weighing heavily on many Americans’ minds, according to the AP Voter Poll. The poll points to a midterm electorate that is deeply unhappy with the country’s direction and pessimistic about the future.
Here's the latest:
Black voter turnout appears robust on Election Day, voter coalition says
LaTosha Brown, co-founder of the voting rights group Black Voters Matter, said turnout in some states seemed to rival that of 2008, when Democrat Barack Obama was running for president for the first time.
She and others said turnout appeared particularly high in Michigan and Mississippi.
Brown, speaking during a media briefing organized by the National Coalition on Black Civic Participation, said her organization had more than 2,000 poll observers in several states. They reported no “widescale issues” for voters, she said.
Melanie Campbell, president and CEO of the coalition, said the group has extended its monitoring efforts beyond Election Day — through vote counting, certifications and even winners’ inaugurations.
“As those of us who believe that this democracy is for all people, we have to also stand in the gap,” she said.
AP Voter Poll: Voters show unhappiness with Trump’s health care policies
Most voters say Trump’s policies made the health and well-being of people in the U.S. worse.
About 2 in 10 say Trump’s policies have improved health and well-being, while 2 in 10 don’t see an impact.
Relatively few voters, about 1 in 10, say health care is the top issue facing the country.
But about half of voters say the president’s policies have made access to health care and the cost of health care worse.
Many Democratic candidates made health care a major issue in their campaigns. In Senate-battleground Michigan, Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed centered his campaign on universal health care.
About 6 in 10 voters say they want the federal government to have a larger role in getting Americans health care.
AP Voter Poll: Ohio Republican Sen. Husted seen as too loyal to Trump
Trump has repeatedly complimented Ohio Sen. Jon Husted for his record in Washington and his physical appearance.
But voters in the Senate race have worries about the former college football star’s willingness to stand up to the president.
About 6 in 10 say Husted is “too supportive” of Trump.
Meanwhile, Ohio voters are split over whether Democrat Sherrod Brown, a former senator, is “too extreme.”
AP Voter Poll: Senate voters in South Carolina have doubts about Darline Graham’s experience
After the July death of Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, his sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to fill the open seat, and she then chose to stand for election.
But voters do not necessarily see Darline Graham as having the same political skills as her brother.
About 6 in 10 Senate voters in South Carolina say Darline Graham does not have the right experience to serve as a senator, though most Republican voters believe she does.
Voters are divided on whether her Democratic opponent, pediatrician Annie Andrews, is “too extreme” in her views.
Civil rights group says ICE social media message intended to intimidate voters
Carmen Feliciano, vice president for policy and advocacy at the Latino civil rights group UnidosUS, criticized U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for a social media post that said, in part: “If you vote illegally, we will find you.”
The agency posted the message on Election Day.
“This is part of a strategy we have been seeing for the last few years — intimidation and trying to block people from going out to the polls,” Feliciano said.
She noted that Latino turnout was expected to be high for the midterm elections.
Asked why the message went out, the Department of Homeland Security, which includes ICE, issued a statement that read in part: “ONLY Americans should elect American leaders.”
Throughout the day, ICE announced arrests or charges against people suspected of voting as noncitizens in previous elections.
AP Voter Poll: In Georgia Senate race, Ossoff seen as less extreme than Collins
Only about 4 in 10 Senate voters in Georgia say Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has views that are “too extreme.”
About half, by contrast, say the views of his opponent, Republican Rep. Mike Collins, are “too extreme.”
Ossoff has accused Collins of employing staffers who are white nationalists. Trump and other Republicans have suggested that Ossoff’s perspectives on immigration and the economy are outside the American mainstream.
Key US House races to watch in Florida
A handful of key U.S. House races in Florida could offer early signs of how Democrats are performing tonight.
Democratic Reps. Darren Soto and Kathy Castor are defending their seats in the redrawn 9th and 14th Districts. Both of the districts would have favored Trump by double-digit margins in the 2024 presidential election.
The 22nd District is an open seat after Democratic Rep. Lois Frankel opted to run in the 23rd District when her district was redrawn.
What to watch for after polls close at 7 pm ET
All polls close at 7 p.m. in six states, including Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia, which tend to complete almost all of their vote counting on election night.
In the 2024 general election, the vote count in all three states reached the halfway mark in the 8 p.m. hour. The counts were 90% complete at 10:21 p.m. in Georgia, 11:14 p.m. in South Carolina and 12:07 a.m. in Virginia. In Georgia’s competitive presidential contest, The Associated Press declared Trump the winner at 12:58 a.m.
Most Florida polls will also close at 7 p.m., including in every competitive congressional district, but no statewide winners will be declared until polls in the Central Time Zone close at 8 p.m.
Polls in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia close at 7:30 p.m. All three states also count votes relatively quickly, reaching the halfway point at around 9 p.m. in 2024 and about 90% in the 11 p.m. hour. The AP declared a winner in Ohio’s competitive 2024 U.S. Senate race at 11:27 p.m.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio; gubernatorial races in Georgia and Ohio; and U.S. House races in Florida, Indiana, South Carolina, Virginia, Ohio and North Carolina.
AP Voter Poll: About half of voters say Trump has gone too far on immigration enforcement
Most voters say they’re not fans of the Trump administration’s aggressive crackdowns on immigration.
About 6 in 10 “somewhat” or “strongly” disapprove of how U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is handling its responsibilities.
Roughly 7 in 10 voters say immigration enforcement was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote for Congress. Although under half, about 4 in 10, say it was “crucial.”
Trump made closing the U.S.-Mexico border to illegal border crossings a priority, but his deployment of federal officers to arrest and deport immigrants stirred protests that led to the deaths of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota.
About 6 in 10 voters say the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement actions have gone too far, while about 2 in 10 say they haven’t gone far enough. About 2 in 10 say his policies are about right.
Flooding strands voters on the Navajo Nation
Hundreds of voters in Rock Point, Arizona, on the Navajo Nation were unable to reach the polls Tuesday as flooding had closed a major bridge and washed out dirt roads, a tribal official said.
On a typical Election Day, the chapter house parking lot would be buzzing with voters, candidates and pop-up food stalls.
“Unfortunately, today that parking lot is underwater,” said Valinda Shirley, vice president of the Rock Point Chapter, the local seat of tribal government.
Officials moved the polling place across the street to an administration building, but many residents remained stranded.
“I have people that are still texting me asking how I can get them out so they can vote,” Shirley said Tuesday afternoon.
The flooding is keeping those residents from casting ballots in both the U.S. midterms and races for Navajo Nation president and council delegates.
Jeffries says House Democrats are ready to deliver the ‘best version’ of America
Jeffries, who’s in line to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if Democrats seize control and elect him to the job, said House Democrats don’t work for any president.
“We work for all of you, the American people, and we’re committed to delivering an America that’s the best version of herself,” he said.
He told the volunteers that Democrats are “committed to ending this national nightmare, fighting to make this country affordable” and “continuing our country’s long, necessary and majestic march toward a more perfect union.”
He urged them on: “Let’s go win this thing.”
AP Voter Poll: Capitalism viewed more positively than socialism
More than half of voters strongly or somewhat favor the free market principles of capitalism.
Only about 3 in 10 feel similarly positive about socialism, in which the government plays a greater role in economic activity.
Trump and other Republicans campaigned on the idea that many Democratic candidates with their plans for universal healthcare were socialist. Democrats countered that the Trump administration had taken ownership stakes in dozens of private companies.
AP Voter Poll shows unhappiness with US military action in Iran
Voters are unhappy with Trump’s war with Iran.
About 6 in 10 voters say the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran. The cost of the unpopular war has risen to more than $47.1 billion, according to a recent estimate from the Pentagon.
Roughly one-third of voters say the Iran war was a “crucial” factor in their vote for Congress, which is lower than the share of those who expressed concern over the cost of living and government corruption.
Trump has asserted that higher gas and energy prices resulting from conflict will drop.
AP Voter Poll: Voters express severe concerns about inflation
About 8 in 10 voters say inflation has caused a “severe” or “moderate” financial hardship on their households.
The drag caused by prices rising faster than wages over the past year has made it harder for many voters to afford basic essentials such as gasoline, groceries and their utilities.
The persistent concern is a carryover from the 2024 presidential election when voters specifically tasked Trump to solve the problem, but inflation is now higher than it was when he returned to the White House.
More than 8 in 10 voters say they are “very” or “somewhat” concerned about the cost of gas, groceries, utilities and healthcare.
Jeffries says Democrats ‘on the brink’ of taking back the House
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries popped by to rally and thank volunteers at a phone bank in Washington for battleground House candidates.
“We’re on the brink of a dramatic change of direction in this country,” Jeffries said.
“We’re on the brink of Democrats taking back control of the House of Representatives.”
He said a Democratic win would be a victory for Americans.
“We’re going to deliver a Congress that actually puts the American people first,” he said.
Democrats are dialing voters in an election evening push for the House
House Democrats have opened a phone bank in Washington with dozens of volunteers calling voters in key House races across the country before polls close.
They’re encouraging voters to cast ballots as Democrats work to wrest control of the House from Republicans.
The AP Voter Poll: Most voters are dissatisfied or angry with the country’s direction
Voters overwhelmingly feel frustrated with the way things are going in the U.S. today, according to The AP Voter Poll, which points to a midterm electorate that is deeply unhappy with the country’s direction and pessimistic about the future.
About three-quarters of voters say they feel “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the country’s current trajectory. Only about one-quarter feel “satisfied” or “enthusiastic.” Dissatisfaction was particularly high in blue states like California and Massachusetts, but even in deep-red states, a majority of voters were at least “dissatisfied.”
Voters are also displeased with the condition of the economy, with roughly three-quarters saying it is “not so good” or “poor.” That’s in line with what U.S. adults have said in recent months in AP-NORC polling.
The AP Voter Poll: The economy and the state of democracy are voters’ top issues
Voters say the economy and the state of democracy are the top issues facing the country, with high costs and government corruption weighing heavily on many Americans’ minds as they cast a ballot in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
About 4 in 10 U.S. voters nationally say the economy is the most important issue facing the country, as most express concern about gas prices and the cost of groceries. About 3 in 10 say the state of democracy is the top issue. Only about 1 in 10 say the same about immigration or health care, and few name foreign policy or crime.
Roughly half of U.S. voters say government corruption and the cost of living are “crucial” to their vote for Congress, much higher than the share who say that about immigration enforcement policies, the war in Iran or AI data centers.
House races to watch: Districts that flipped in 2024
The handful of House members who flipped the toughest seats in 2024 all face challenging races again this year. Can they avoid a sophomore slump?
Most of these districts flipped to the GOP in 2024, riding Trump’s coattails as he clinched a second term. The good news for these Republicans is that it’s almost always easier to win a seat that you already represent. The bad news is that many of them won their seats by tiny margins and are facing a much tougher national environment this time around.
See other House races to watch in the AP’s guide to battleground congressional districts here.
The AP Voter Poll: Most voters believe Trump’s policies have harmed the US economy
Relatively few voters have positive things to say about Trump’s economic leadership.
About two-thirds of U.S. midterm voters say Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S., while only about 3 in 10 say they’ve improved things. Similarly, about two-thirds of voters said Trump’s tariff policies have hurt the national economy.
Views of Trump’s priorities more broadly — and his capabilities as a leader — are also mostly negative. More than half of voters say Trump is not a strong leader, does not fight for people like them, does not have the right priorities and does not have the mental capability to serve effectively as president.
About 6 in 10 voters said Trump places a higher priority on his own personal interests than the country’s interests, while about 4 in 10 said he puts more weight on the country’s interests.
DOJ escalates criminal investigation of Alaska Senate candidate
The Trump administration notified prominent Democratic attorney Marc Elias and others that they may be targets of the inquiry, which focuses on a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.
That’s according to two people familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.
Trump’s DOJ is investigating retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan’s decision to run for Senate, which the president says will confuse voters because he shares a first and last name with Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan. The New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan.
“This administration has repeatedly weaponized the DOJ against the President’s political enemies despite zero evidence of wrongdoing, and we are the latest targets,” Elias said in a statement Tuesday.
The AP Voter Poll: Voters want Congress to impose more checks on an unpopular president
Most voters want to see Congress provide more checks and balances on the presidency and disapprove of how Congress is handling its job.
The AP Voter Poll shows roughly 7 in 10 voters say Congress is doing “not enough” to provide checks and balances on the presidency. Only about 2 in 10 say it’s doing “about the right amount,” and about 1 in 10 say Congress is doing “too much.”
The survey reflects deep unhappiness with the president and Congress. About 6 in 10 voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the presidency, while about three-quarters of voters disapprove of the way Congress is handling its job.
Cost of living, corruption top issues and voters deeply unhappy with Trump: Early election takeaways
Voters are in the mood for change, according to the AP Voter Poll, which found that roughly three-quarters of voters say they feel “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the way things are going in the country today. Most appear to blame the Trump administration for high costs. About 6 in 10 say higher-than-usual prices are “more because of Trump’s policies” rather than “more because of factors outside Trump’s control.”
Additionally, about 70% of voters want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the presidency.
The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of the electorate, suggests most are deeply unhappy with Trump, with roughly 6 in 10 saying they disapprove of how he’s handling the presidency.
About 4 in 10 say the economy is the most important issue facing the country, while 3 in 10 say the most important issue is democracy, according to the poll, well above the number who said the same about crime, health care and immigration.
Immigration enforcement agency issues warning to voters
Federal immigration officials took to social media on Election Day to warn against illegal voting by noncitizens.
In a message on X, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement wrote: “If you vote illegally, we will find you. We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you. There will be no escape.”
The agency did not return messages seeking comment about the post. Throughout Tuesday, it also posted about arrests of noncitizens accused of voting.
While that has been a major emphasis for the agency this year, the number of arrests and earlier investigations in the states demonstrate the problem is rare.
David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, called the post unfortunate but said heavy early voting suggested the administration’s tactics appeared to have no effect on turnout.
“If there were individuals in this administration who thought that they could scare voters away from this election, they’re going to be disappointed,” he said.
Incumbents in redrawn districts face very different electorates than in 2024
Many incumbents running for reelection in redrawn districts are facing a very different set of voters than they currently represent.
Several districts went from being majority-nonwhite to majority-white after mid-decade redistricting. These are also some of the places that shifted the most toward Trump when comparing the 2024 vote margin under old and new congressional boundaries.
Similarly, a number of districts shifted from being majority-white to being majority-nonwhite. Many of these districts also shifted toward Harris, but some in Texas and Florida moved further to the right.
Latest views on the 2 major parties from AP-NORC polling
At least half of U.S. adults have a negative opinion of the two parties, according to AP-NORC polling.
About half have a “very” or “somewhat” unfavorable view of the Democratic Party in an AP-NORC poll from October, while just over half say that about the Republican Party.
Roughly 7 in 10 Democrats hold a favorable view of their own party, which is down from 85% in September 2024. Republicans, however, feel about as positively as they did two years ago, with 85% in the latest polling saying they have a favorable view of the Republican Party.
Only about 2 in 10 U.S. adults feel “very” or “somewhat” optimistic about the future of the Democratic Party or the Republican Party. Republicans are a bit more optimistic about their party’s future than Democrats are — slightly fewer than half of Republicans, 46%, say they are feeling positive, compared to 35% of Democrats.

Voting gets underway in US Midterms, pollsters predict gains for Democrats in Senate and House - The Tribune
sources.text:
Washington DC [US], November 3 (ANI): More than 230 million eligible voters in the United States are heading to the polls across the nation as voting gets underway in the 2026 midterm elections, a high-stakes referendum on the second half of President Donald Trump's term that will determine the balance of power in Washington.
With all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats on the ballot, major pollsters and forecasting models project key potential gains for Democrats, who are seeking to capture the narrow majorities needed to take back control of both chambers of Congress.
Democrats hold advantages over Republicans in nearly all of the seven key battleground states that will determine control of the US Senate, according to the latest set of pre-midterm election polls released by The New York Times and Siena University.
The polling highlights notable Democratic strength in traditional Republican territory. Surveys show Democratic candidates holding sizable leads in Texas, a state that has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, as well as Kansas, which last elected a Democratic senator in 1932.
Reclaiming a Senate majority presents a challenging path for Democrats. To secure control, the party must defend every seat it currently holds while successfully flipping at least four Republican-held seats, an undertaking widely viewed as an uphill battle given that several targeted contests are located in deep-red strongholds.
Despite those obstacles, the latest survey data indicates Democratic candidates are leading in five states currently represented by Republican senators and are effectively tied in a sixth. Democratic contenders hold leads in Kansas, Maine, Ohio, and Texas, alongside a narrow edge in Alaska, while remaining effectively tied in Iowa.
Nationally, voter dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump and frustration over his economic management continue to drag down Republican candidates. According to the polling, just 38 per cent of likely voters approved of the president's performance.
Earlier in the day, American Statistician Nate Silver and the FLIPR 2026 midterm election forecast said Democratic candidates are leading in polling averages across every major battleground state, including Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Maine and Iowa.
The forecast gives Democrats a 3.3-percentage-point advantage in Texas, a three-point lead in Ohio, 4.9 points in Michigan, 3.9 points in Maine and 1.1 points in Iowa.
Georgia and North Carolina, meanwhile, barely register as competitive in the forecast, while the Democratic candidate in the Kansas Senate race is leading by four percentage points in polling averages.
Along with the seats in the House of Representatives and Senate, voters in 36 states will also elect their governors. Republicans currently control both chambers of Congress.
More than 57 million Americans have already cast their ballots through early voting, as per ABC News, with voters also able to participate through mail-in voting or in person today.
Meanwhile, the US Department of Justice has released a comprehensive list of locations where it intends to send election observers, marking what the agency describes as the largest federal monitoring initiative in American history.
ABC News reports that the Justice Department’s official statement outlines plans to dispatch approximately 1,000 monitors spanning all 50 states. However, an official testified during a court hearing that the actual deployment would likely be closer to 900 personnel due to initial challenges in identifying and training sufficient staff in time for Election Day.
Deploying election observers is a standard practice across presidential administrations, with staff typically drawn from the Voting Section of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division. Nonetheless, ABC News notes that these operational announcements have faced growing pushback from Democratic critics in recent months, fueled by concerns over the Trump administration's aggressive efforts to obtain voter registry data aimed at detecting noncitizen registration.
Several closely watched Senate contests are also taking place across the country as both parties compete for control of the upper chamber.
In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is facing Republican Mike Rogers in a closely watched contest, following Democratic Representative Haley Stevens' decision to endorse Rogers on Sunday.
In Florida, Democrat Angie Nixon is challenging Republican Senator Ashley Moody, while Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is facing Republican Mike Collins.
Maine Republican Senator Susan Collins is contesting against Democrat Troy Jackson, while in New Hampshire, Democratic Representative Chris Pappas is on the ballot against former Republican Senator John Sununu.
In North Carolina, Democrat Roy Cooper and Republican Michael Whatley are competing for the Senate seat.
The first election results could begin emerging on Tuesday as polling stations close across different states. Vote counting will continue throughout Tuesday evening and into Wednesday as election officials process ballots and release results.
However, the final outcome in several contests may take longer to establish, as mail-in, provisional and other ballots are often counted after election night. Consequently, the final vote tallies could take several days or even weeks to be completed.
With Republicans currently holding majorities in both chambers, theoutcome of the elections will determine which party controls Congress for the next two years. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the Senate and three seats in the House of Representatives to secure majorities in the respective chambers. (ANI)

The races to watch in US midterms
Four ‘toss-up’ Senate seats could decide who wields power in Washington
US voters head to the polls today for midterm elections billed as a referendum on Donald Trump, even though the president’s name will not appear on a single ballot.
Up for grabs are all 435 seats in the lower house of Congress – the House of Representatives, where the Democrats expect to secure a majority – as well as 35 out of the 100 seats in the Senate, where the competition is predicted to be far closer.
Democrats would need to win four of seven Senate races deemed to be a “toss-up” by independent elections analyst The Cook Political Report to give them control of Congress, and with it “the power to limit Trump’s ambitions, reject his judicial nominations and investigate his administration”, said the BBC. Here are the races to watch:

Michigan
Probably the most hard-fought and vitriolic Senate race in this election cycle. Republicans have tried to paint Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed as a socialist and an Islamic extremist with links to the Muslim Brotherhood. Polls have remained neck-and-neck but a late shock endorsement for Republican challenger Mike Rogers by Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, could have a decisive impact. Crucially, this is one of the few toss-up Senate seats currently held by the Democrats, and winning it back would be a boost to Republican hopes of clinging on to a majority in Congress.
Alaska
Democrat candidate Mary Peltola, the first Indigenous Alaskan to be elected to the House of Representatives, has campaigned for the Senate on a platform of “fish, family, freedom” to come within touching distance of flipping the Republican seat.
While Alaska’s ranked-choice system has historically made it harder for pollsters to predict the winner, the election campaign has also been marred by controversy and accusations of dirty tricks with the appearance of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. One is the incumbent Republican senator, the other a retired teacher with no prior political experience, sparking claims he had been induced to run by the senator’s opponents in the hopes of confusing voters.
Texas
The Lone Star state has not sent a Democrat to the Senate in nearly 40 years, but polls show rising star James Talarico is in with a fighting chance. At more than half a billion dollars and counting, it is the most expensive Senate race in US history, with Republican challenger and arch-Trump loyalist Attorney General Ken Paxton trying to paint his opponent – who once suggested God was non-binary – as far-left on culture issues. But Talarico, a 37-year-old former teacher who studied to be a Christian minister, has nonetheless managed to cut through with voters in the traditionally deep-red Republican stronghold.

Kansas
Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, but rising farming and fuel costs linked to Trump’s war in Iran, as well as the impact of the president’s immigration crackdown on rural businesses, means the state is unexpectedly up for grabs. The Democrats have also benefited from picking charismatic Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton as their candidate in a state with a large evangelical and mainline Protestant population. As Election Day arrives, Democrats poised to see gains and pump brakes on Trump agenda
Early voting at Kearny Town Hall in Kearny, New Jersey, on Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
WASHINGTON — Tens of millions of Americans have already cast a ballot in the 2026 midterm elections that will determine control of Congress and shape President Donald Trump’s remaining policy agenda.
As of Monday, more than 57 million Americans had cast a vote, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, which tracks early voting. This year’s elections have already shattered the record for midterm early voting, set in 2022, in which nearly 46 million Americans voted early.
Polls close between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m. local time on Election Day. Under federal law, as long as voters are in line when the polls close, they can still cast their ballots. Voters must be at least 18 years old, a U.S. citizen and registered to vote in their state. Many states allow same-day registration.
Trump came into his second term with his party in control of both chambers of Congress. But historically, the president’s party loses seats in the midterm elections, and this cycle appears unlikely to be an exception.
Elections forecasters have favored Democrats to win back the majority in the U.S. House, which would allow them to significantly rein in Trump’s legislative agenda. Analysts have also increasingly predicted Democrats could win control of the U.S. Senate could, which would allow them to block appointments, including a potential U.S. Supreme Court vacancy.
The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter projects Democrats to pick up a Senate seat in North Carolina and lists six more races as toss-ups, all of which are now held by Republicans. Those races are in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio and Texas. Democrats are defending an open seat in Michigan that the Cook Political Report moved from toss-up to leaning toward the Democrat, Abdul El-Sayed, on Monday.
If the other races go as predicted, Democrats would have to win at least three of the toss-ups to gain control of the chamber.
The Cook Political Report shifted 12 House races in the direction of Democrats on Oct. 30. Eighteen remained toss-ups as of Monday. Democrats have to net three seats to flip control of the House, if they also win the race in a heavily Democratic Florida district that is vacant after former Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick resigned in April.
If Democrats gain the majority in the House, they are likely to pursue investigations into Trump and other administration officials.
They have also signaled they will embrace a policy agenda centered on lowering costs, especially related to healthcare, though Trump’s veto looms on any major legislation Congress passes for the next two years.
Legal challenges amid dismal numbers
The war with Iran that has contributed to high gas and diesel prices, inflation and an aggressive immigration crackdown has led to historically low presidential approval ratings. Trump’s approval on average was at 37% Monday, only a tick better than his second-term low of 36% recorded just two weeks earlier, according to The New York Times.
The president has already made an attempt to use the Department of Justice to halt the certification of the Alaska U.S. Senate race, after The New York Times reported the campaign of Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola made an effort to recruit a candidate with the same name as GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan in order to stack the four-way general election in her favor.
States Newsroom has not independently verified the Times story.
A federal judge tossed out the lawsuit Sunday.
Other court challenges related to the administration’s actions or potential actions related to the election are still unfolding on Election Day. Cases include Democrats’ aim to bar armed federal officials for polling locations and DOJ’s effort to prevent California from counting 20,000 votes the Trump administration suspects are noncitizens.
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday denied the Trump administration’s final attempt to force California to set aside the ballots.
Separately, congressional Democrats have taken their own precautions. More than 100 Senate staffers and 300 House staffers were trained as election monitors and will be sent to 60 or 70 close races, the top Democrat on the House Administration Committee, Joe Morelle, told reporters last week.
Even after the polls close, it could take weeks to know the results of some races, and consequently, control of both chambers of Congress, due to each state’s voting laws and processes for counting votes.
After the 2022 midterms, control of the House was projected for Republicans eight days after Election Day. In 2024, the same projection took nine days.

sources.news_title: Will Democrats deliver a blue wave? Here’s how to parse tonight’s election results like a pro. - The Boston Globe
