American politics may be unpredictable, but election nights tend to follow a pattern. Amid the noise, scattered results, and endless hot takes, a handful of early signals can tell you whether the night is unfolding as expected — or whether one party is headed for a wave.
This guide draws on the patterns of recent election cycles to help you separate the meaningful signals from the noise from your group chat, and the silly people on television (like me, who is scheduled to appear on NBC’s national election night broadcast).
By the numbers
3 — The number of House seats Democrats need to flip to gain the majority.
81 — The number of competitive House seats, according to the Cook Political Report.
4 — The number of competitive Senate seats Democrats must continue to hold: New Hampshire, Georgia, Michigan, and Minnesota.
If they do, then:
4 — The number of states they must flip to gain the Senate majority. By definition, two of these states will have to be places Donald Trump won by more than 10 points just two years ago.
The times
6 p.m.: First polls close.
7 p.m.: First competitive Senate polls close.
8 p.m.: Polls close in Massachusetts.
9 p.m.: First sense of whether it’s a massive wave year, based on scattered election results.
9:30 p.m.: First competitive races are called.
11 p.m.: The waiting begins.
End of the week: When we actually know which party won the Senate.
The vibes
Heading into the election, the conventional wisdom is that Democrats will have a good night. Almost everyone believes Democrats will win the House majority; the question is by how much. Democrats would like a comfortable buffer so they aren’t beholden to a small faction of either moderates or newly elected Democratic Socialists.
The Senate is a different story. Georgia Senator Raphael Warnock, a Democrat, recently conceded that he thinks the best Democrats can do is 52 seats, one more than they need. He has been out campaigning in battleground states.
The caveat
This was written and edited before Election Day. If there are any significant hijinks involving voting or voters, that’s not factored in below and, frankly, we have bigger problems.
6pm: Exit polls
I wanted to require that every reader of this article raise their right hand and pledge to do anything else with their life besides read and discuss exit polls starting around dinner time. They are basically useless in midterms, especially this midterm. But you can lower your right hand because there is one exit poll data point that matters: Did Republicans vote?
This election has uncanny similarities to 2006, when Democrats had a big wave year largely because disillusioned Republicans stayed home. Nine of the top 10 Senate battlegrounds are in historically Republican states where, if Republicans vote, Republicans win.
In midterms, it’s less about convincing voters to switch parties than getting out the base. Democrats are motivated; Republicans are less so. The question is how much that turnout gap matters — and exit polls aren’t particularly good at measuring it, especially in states with few recent competitive elections. Take Kansas, which hasn’t had a competitive Senate general election since 1974, when Republican Bob Dole won reelection by only 1.7 percentage points. (Use that factoid to impress your friends.)
6pm: A place called Kokomo (and Lexington)
Chances are you have no idea where Kokomo is located. For those of you familiar with the Beach Boys song with that title, sorry, it’s not a tropical island. Instead, it’s a down-at-the-heels industrial town in central Indiana.
It’s also where the story of the 2026 midterm elections begins.
Indiana and Kentucky are the first states in the nation to close their polls, doing so promptly at 6 p.m. Eastern. There is an open House seat in Louisville that is considered a toss-up. That’s interesting enough. But if the central question is how big — and whether there will be — a blue wave, the first data point we have to answer it comes from Indiana’s Fifth Congressional District.
Republican incumbent Victoria Spartz is seeking reelection. She is, well, complicated. She was an annoying holdout vote in an epic House speaker race in 2025 before she flipped. Born in Ukraine, she supported President Volodymyr Zelensky before turning against him. Heck, she announced she wasn’t seeking reelection in 2024, before changing her mind. She has one of the highest staff turnover rates in Congress because she is apparently difficult to work with.
But let’s leave all that aside, since it really isn’t driving the contest. Trump is driving the contest. This is a district dominated by educated Indianapolis suburbs, mixed with rural areas that make it more GOP friendly. The Cook Political Report rates her race as “likely Republican,” making it a great place to test the wave theory. Trump won the district by 19 points two years ago. The latest poll shows the race within the margin of error.
If Spartz loses early in the night, a LOT of Republicans around the country are going to lose along with her.
7pm South Carolina and New Hampshire
Around then, we should have a better idea of how the first two competitive Senate races are going, if they haven’t already been called.
In New Hampshire, Democrats need to hold the Senate seat, and most polls show Representative Chris Pappas doing that against Republican John E. Sununu, who held this very seat. (Fun fact: If Sununu wins, it will set a record for the longest gap before a senator returns to the Senate — 18 years.)
The real tell will be in South Carolina, where Republican Darline Graham is running in place of her deceased brother, Lindsey Graham. She has, at times, come across as a lightweight, saying that “national security is not my thing,” while her Democratic opponent, Annie Andrews, has momentum and has tied the race.
South Carolina does tend to count votes more quickly.
Note: New England’s hottest race — Maine’s Senate contest — is purposefully omitted here. In 2020, Republican Susan Collins won by a comfortable 7 points, but wasn’t declared the winner until Wednesday. The race is expected to be closer this time (no matter who wins) and likely no winner will be declared on election night. At least that’s the current thinking. We can always be surprised.
8pm: Florida, Florida, Florida
No one is really talking about Florida this year, but it could be the sneaky story of the entire election. Yes, I am talking about Florida, where I argued in 2022 that Republicans had their biggest wins in the entire country.
It could be where Democrats have their biggest wins in 2026. Florida could matter a great deal and tell us a lot early, given that the state counts its votes quickly. There is an open governor’s race where the Democrat may win. There is also the Senate race, where Republican Ashley Moody (appointed to serve out Marco Rubio’s term) is a lackluster incumbent but faces a Democratic Socialist, making a Democratic win seem like a reach.
So, for our purposes, let’s talk about Florida’s 28 House races. A last-minute redistricting measure earlier this year aimed to take away four Democratic seats. But the districts were drawn for Republicans to have a 5-point advantage. That’s more than enough in a normal year, but in 2026 this could be a problem. Currently, Democrats nationally are up 9 points in the House vote. If that plays out in Florida, then instead of Republicans picking up four seats, they could lose 10. That alone would be enough to take back the House and then some.
11pm: Choose your adventure
It’s at this point that you, dear reader, have a decision to make. There is going to be a lot of waiting for a lot of results. You can call your friends, grab something to drink, or go to bed.
Me? I am going to bed.
Overall, we are looking at tight Senate contests all over the country that will require a lot of counting and possibly even recounts. Indeed, it could all come down to Alaska’s Senate contest, which historically has taken weeks. No one wants that, of course, but there is also no point in staying up for it.
James Pindell is a Globe political reporter who reports and analyzes American politics, especially in New England.

sources.news_title: When do polls open and close in Ohio on Election Day?
US midterm elections live updates: Voting begins with Trump’s Republicans behind in key polls
sources.text:
Main Points
- Voters in the United States are electing members of Congress, which is made up of two parts – the House of Representatives and the Senate.
- Polls have closed in Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, South Carolina, Vermont, Virginia
- The outcome will determine which political party – Donald Trump’s Republicans or opposition Democrats – controls Congress and how easily the US president can advance his agenda.
- Unofficial results published by the Guam Election Commission show that Republican candidate Vicente Ada was elected as governor of Guam.
Key Reads
- What are the US midterms and what do they mean for Donald Trump?
- US midterm election night: When Irish viewers can expect key calls
- Keith Duggan: Trump proclaims ‘golden age’ while US midterm polls are flashing historical defeats
- Analysis: The US midterms show a blue surge. Can we trust them?
Democrat Jon Ossoff projected to win re-election in Georgia senate race
Democrat Jon Ossoff is projected to win re-election in the Georgia Senate race, according to NBC News.
Georgia was rated by analysts as a Democrat-leaning state, so it’s not a big surprise. It was one of the few states where Democrats had a money advantage in the final stretch and had moved off the board for Republicans.
Our Washington Correspondent Keith Duggan recently profiled Ossoff, an emerging Democrat star who has become a chief thorn in Trump’s side.
Polls close in six states
Polls have closed in Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, South Carolina, Vermont, Virginia
These are the first states to finish voting. The next batch of poll closures will take place at 12:30am Irish time in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia.
Meanwhile, some of the TV networks are making their first projections.
NBC projects Democrat Mark Warner will defeat Republican Bert Mizusawa to win another term in the Virginia senate race. Virginia is a solidly Democratic state, so no big surprise there.
NBC also projects Republican politician Hal Rogers will win re-election in Kentucky’s 5th congressional district, rated as a solidly Republican district by analysts.
Meanwhile, Democrat Morgan McGarvey is projected to win Kentucky’s 3rd congressional district, rated as solidly Democratic district by analysts.
These results offer an early snapshot of the contests shaping the battle for control of Congress.
What does turnout typically look like in US midterm elections?
Turnout tends to be lower in US midterm elections than in the presidential elections.
Turnout in the last two midterms was 52 per cent in 2022 and 53 per cent in 2018, according to the US Census Bureau.
But with the presidency on the ballot, 65 per cent of eligible voters turned out in 2024 and 67 per cent in 2020.
Latest opinion polls indicate that Democratic voters are more likely to turn out than Republicans this year.
Election analysts have cautioned that such Democratic constituencies as young, Black and Hispanic voters have historically turned out at lower rates in midterm elections.
And surveys show persistent skepticism among these groups towards both parties, especially over the cost of living.
If turnout among those groups falls short of expectations, Democrats could underperform on election day.
Was Trump’s election day announcement on cutting aid to Israel a sign of desperation?
Earlier on Tuesday, US president Trump made a surprise election day announcement on US aid to Israel, a topic that has been raised in some midterm campaigns.
He said he had made a deal with Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion in funding to Israel after the end of this year, though it would still sell Israel weapons.
The announcement comes as US public support for Israel has fallen, particularly among Democrats, since Israel’s harsh response in Gaza to a deadly Hamas-led cross-border attack in October 2023.
Trump did not say why he chose to announce the deal on Tuesday, but a number of candidates critical of Israel won Democratic primaries over the past year, and even moderate candidates have been increasingly willing to challenge longtime US support.
In a key battleground race, Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed is seeking to represent Michigan in the US senate. El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim to serve as a US senator, has opposed unconditional military aid to Israel.
First polls close in Indiana and Kentucky
The first polls in the 2026 US midterms have closed now in Indiana and Kentucky.
Kentucky’s 6th district, an open seat rated by many as a toss-up, is being treated by analysts as an early test of whether a large Democratic wave is building.
At midnight, polls in Virginia, Georgia, South Carolina and most of Florida will close. Virginia’s 2nd district will be the first genuine swing seat to report.
My colleague Hugh Linehan has provided this guide on when to expect the key calls.
How will the TV networks project results?
Most TV networks and web outlets rely on two providers for vote counts: the Associated Press (AP) or election data firm Decision Desk HQ.
Some news outlets like Fox News and CBS News make their own projections based on the AP vote count, exit polls, early-vote totals and their own statistical modeling.
The first projections will start soon after polls begin to close, first with Indiana and Kentucky at 11pm Irish time.
Then, polls close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia at midnight Irish time.
When making calls, the AP says it uses vote totals and estimates how many votes remain uncounted based on past voting patterns and early-vote data.
It calls a race only when the trailing candidate cannot catch up.
Decision Desk HQ collects vote counts from official state sources. The firm says it uses statistical analysis, modeling and expert review to project election winners.
Most voters ‘angry’ or ‘dissatisfied’ with direction of US
Voters are in the mood for change, according to the AP Voter Poll, which found that roughly three-quarters of voters say they feel “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the way things are going in the country today.
The poll finds most appear to blame the Trump administration for high costs. About six in 10 say higher-than-usual prices are “more because of Trump’s policies” rather than “more because of factors outside Trump’s control.”
Additionally, about 70 per cent of voters want the US Congress to provide more checks and balances on the presidency.
The AP poll suggests most are deeply unhappy with Trump, with roughly six in 10 saying they disapprove of how he’s handling the presidency.
About four in 10 say the economy is the most important issue facing the country, while three in 10 say the most important issue is democracy, according to the poll, well above the number who said the same about crime, health care and immigration.
US midterm polls show a blue surge. Can we trust them?
Democrats are leading in all key states that will decide senate control, according to the latest polls.
However, surveys have underestimated Trump and Republican support before.
There’s precedent in the Trump era for polls to overestimate Democrats, and it’s reasonable to wonder whether the polls might be overestimating Democratic strength yet again. Statistically, Republicans more likely not to respond to polls, which introduces the ever-present risk of a polling misfire.
The political analyst Nate Cohn says the latest New York Times/Siena polls have been weighted to take account of this.
In addition, he argues Democrats lead by enough that they could win the Senate even if the polls underestimate Republicans by as much as they did in 2016 or 2020.
Minnesota voters remember US citizens killed by federal immigration officials
Minnesota voters left “I Voted” stickers on memorial sites for Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, the two US citizens killed by federal immigration officials earlier this year.
Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care unit nurse at the Veterans Affairs medical center in Minneapolis, Minnesota, and Good, a writer and mother of three, were killed during a large-scale immigration enforcement operation in the Minneapolis region in January.
Republican voters outnumber Democrats in all votes cast
In voting on Tuesday, Republican voters outnumbered Democrats by almost half, 856,000 to 445,000, according to Florida Vote Tracker.
In all votes cast, Republicans led 3.06 million to 2.5 million, with another 1.6 million independent or no party affiliated votes cast.
The figures, of course, reflect only the number of returned votes by affiliation so far, not who voters actually voted for.
Technical issues reported in several areas
In New York state, Westchester county executive Kenneth Jenkins told a news conference that voting machines have been unable to scan as many as 250,000 ballots in 332 polling locations across more than 40 of the county’s municipalities.
Jenkins stressed that people will still be able to vote, and would be directed to cast their vote on emergency ballots.
Technical issues were reported across several Mississippi counties.
People have experienced issues with voting, according to Mississippi Voters Action Fund, which supports voting in the state.
Election officials in Florida’s Broward county, the largest Democratic party stronghold in the state, say they have resolved issues with voting machines in a number of precincts that prevented early election day voters from casting their ballots.
Joe Scott, the county’s supervisor of elections, said in a statement that the technical problems, which became evident as soon as polling opened, were quickly ironed out.
Voter turnout surges past 2022 levels
Voter turnout has surged in the lead up to this year’s midterm election, with the number of early ballots cast significantly outstripping the totals from the 2022 midterm.
By the afternoon, Florida’s Division of Elections reported more than 1,860,000 votes had been cast on election day.
Georgia’s secretary of state Brad Raffensperger said 775,000 votes had been cast, with an expected total turnout of 1.4 million votes by the close of polling.
Guam elects Republican governor in first unofficial results
The first election results of the 2026 midterms have come in from Guam, the Pacific island territory.
The unofficial results published by the Guam Election Commission show that Republican candidate Vicente Ada (also known as Tony) was elected as governor of Guam.
Voters opted to send Democratic candidate Alicia Anne Garrido Limtiaco to Washington as the delegate to congress.
President Donald Trump took to his personal social media platform to remark on the results, which he considered a strong showing for the Republicans.
“Guam, which has always been considered strongly Democrat, just had an early call for a REPUBLICAN victory in the top spot, Governor — Congratulations to Tony Ada.
“Also, the Republicans have the majority in the State Senate. Wow, hopefully that’s an indication for things to come.”
Officials in some states report strong turnout in opening hours
Voter turnout has surged in the lead up to this year’s midterm election, with the number of early ballots cast significantly outstripping the totals from the 2022 midterm.
Elections workers across the country were expecting that trend to continue into election day.
Officials in states including North Carolina, Georgia, and Michigan reported strong turnout in the opening hours of voting.
When can Irish viewers expect the key calls?
With Ireland five hours ahead of the east coast, the first US midterm polls will close at 11pm our time. But that’s only half the story, writes Hugh Linehan.
Florida and North Carolina usually count most of their vote within hours. Pennsylvania and Wisconsin can’t process postal ballots until polling day, and California accepts postal ballots arriving up to a week late.
A candidate leading at 2am may be trailing by breakfast, and that is normal rather than sinister. If Democrats run ahead of their polls in Virginia, South Carolina and Ohio before 1am, Republicans face a very bad night.
If they don’t, the US Senate may come down to Maine and Alaska, where ranked choice voting slows everything down, and we might not have a definitive result for days or even weeks.
Read the full article here.
US to cut $4 billion in aid to Israel this year, says Trump
President Donald Trump said he had an agreement with Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu to cut off $4 billion in annual US aid.
“Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal,” Trump said in an interview on Tuesday on Fox News.
“We give Israel $4 billion a year and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping — and they’re fine with it.”
“They’ve become a very successful country. They don’t need it. And we won’t be paying anymore,” he added.
Astronauts For America write open letter to US voters
Astronauts For America, an alliance of more than 100 former Nasa explorers, has written an election day open letter to US voters reminding them of the importance of their vote in defending constitutional principles against threats to democracy.
“Federal authority is not a license for any president or federal agency to take over state election administration,” the letter, also signed by ther non-partisan, pro-democracy groups National Security Leaders for America and Leadership Now, said.
“Regardless of political party or personal beliefs, every American should be able to trust that elections are conducted according to the law, every lawful vote is counted, and the results are determined through established legal procedures - not political pressure or the arbitrary exercise of power.”
The letter is a thinly-veiled attack on Donald Trump’s efforts to interfere in election machinery, such as his failed attempts to segregate ballots in California and block certification in the Alaska US senate race. - Guardian
Republicans return more ballots than Democrats in Florida so far
Florida election officials released early voting figures on Tuesday showing registered Republicans in the state returned over 250,000 more ballots than Democrats - 1.49 million to 1.21m.
Gas climbs to election day high of over $4 in bad timing for Republicans
Americans driving to the polls will pay gas prices averaging over $4 a gallon for the first time on record on an election day, the latest milestone in an energy crisis that has taken center stage in the US midterms.
US gas prices averaged $4.13 a gallon as of 10am EST, according to GasBuddy, a fuel savings app.
That’s the most expensive price ever recorded on November 3rd of any year. It’s also more expensive than any prior election day, including 2022, the year US gas prices set an all-time record, according to Patrick De Haan, GasBuddy’s head of petroleum analysis.
The prices today are below the highs set this year of over $4.56 a gallon in May, and they’re down from a national average near $4.50 in late September, according to AAA.
But the $4 price tag has never stuck on gas station marquees so late into the year, the result of snarled global energy shipments and a refining crisis spurred by the US-Iran war, continued Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries and limited exports from China.
In the hours before polls opened, federal judges issued a series of rulings restricting the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to pressure state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting.
The administration’s legal losing streak continued last night. In Washington, one federal judge blocked the administration from demanding officials in California not count any ballots received from people on a list of alleged noncitizens, while another judge prevented the administration from sending such lists to officials in any state.
In San Francisco, the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a lower court order for the administration to stop threatening election officials with prosecution if they did not comply with its demands over alleged noncitizen voters.
Those rulings all came after the US Supreme Court swiftly rejected the administration’s request that it intervene in a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to order California election officials not to count any mail ballots received from more than 20,000 people it says may be noncitizens.
The people have the power, says Kamala Harris.
Now, for the sake of balance, we should probably post something from a Republican perspective and who better to choose but the man who leads that party?
The eight Senate seats to watch tonight
While there are hundreds of races reaching their climax this evening, the outcome may well depend on just eight Senate seats.
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat, is running against Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers, in Michigan while in Maine, Republican incumbent Susan Collins is battlind hard for her seat.
In Alaska, former Democratic congresswoman Mary Peltola will hope to take Republican Dan Sullivan’s seat. In Ohio Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, is hoping to return to the Senate having lost his seat in 2024 while in Texas, James Talarico, is trying to flip a red seat blue with a triumph over Ken Paxton.
Kansas is closer than might have been expected with Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton ahead in the polls against Republican incumbent Roger Marshall while in South Carolina, Darline Graham, the sister of late Senator Lindsey Graham, is running for a full term with polls showing a potentially close contest between her and Democratic nominee Annie Andrews.
And then there is Iowa: With Republican Senator Joni Ernst having vacated her seat, her party’s nominee, congresswoman Ashley Hinson, the GOP in nominee, is running to replace her. She’s up against Democrat Josh Turek, a state lawmaker, in a toss-up contest.
America decides... but when will we know what it’s saying?
While Irish polling booths close at 10pm on the day of voting with the full results not becoming clear for days, they do things differently in the US and many of the polls wil be closing at 6pm local time – or 11pm Irish time - and by early tomorrow morning we should have a good idea what happened. Hugh Linehan has a good breakdown of what we can expect and when we can expect it.
Justice department deploying 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states
The US justice department has said it is deploying 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states in what it called the largest election day monitoring effort in history.
A department statement identified which jurisdictions within the states would receive monitors and observers, and said priorities include areas with a history of voter access issues and places with competitive races that could be targets of voter intimidation.
The Trump administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics view the moves as federal overreach.
Odds on Democrats to come out on top
Many of the polls are pointing to heavy losses for the Republicans, but what about the betting markets?
There has been a staggering $1.48 billion (€1.32 billion) wagered on the midterms on prediction markets such as Kalshi and Polymarket.
The platforms rose to prominence in 2024 when they bucked traditional opinion polls in signalling that Donald Trump would win the presidency, and have since amassed a global following among media outlets and investors.
On Monday, prediction market prices aggregated by analytics firm BetInt implied Democrats had a 95 per cent chance of taking the House of Representatives and a 76 cent chance of taking the Senate.
What is occupying the minds of US voters as they go to the polls?
The rising cost of living will be top of mind for Americans but it is not the only thing concerning them, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that was conducted between last Thursday and Monday.
THE COST OF LIVING
Some 48 per cent of registered voters in the poll say the cost of living is the top issue for deciding how they will vote, compared with 26 per cent who say democratic norms and 13 per cent who point to immigration. US fuel prices have surged since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in February.
DONALD TRUMP
Trump has urged supporters to pretend he is on the ballot in an effort to energize his Republican Party. The Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that 48 per cent of people who planned to vote – or already had done so – said they thought of their ballots as a vote against Trump, compared with 25 per cent who said they were voting for him. Some 25 per cent said Trump was not a factor in their vote.
IRAN
Trump has argued that war was necessary to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons. Some 25 per cent of voters think military action has been worth the cost, and 55 per cent say it has not been worth it with 18 per cent unsure.
ELECTION INTEGRITY
Voters overall trust the US electoral process, with 77 per cent saying they are confident their ballots will be counted but 45 per cent saying they think voter fraud is a widespread problem. Trump has falsely claimed that massive numbers of non-citizens vote illegally and election officials worry the administration could disrupt the election or certification of results it views unfavourably. The White House says its goal is to safeguard election integrity and voting security.
HOUSEHOLD FINANCES
All told 49 per cent of Americans think their household finances have gotten worse since January 2025, when Trump returned to power, compared with 13 per cent who said their finances have gotten better and 37 per cent who say things are about the same. Trump campaigned ahead of the November 2024 presidential election with a promise to turbocharge the economy, but his presidential approval has fallen in recent months to the lowest levels of his political career, including among Hispanic Americans who swung in his direction in 2024. The latest poll showed 54 per cent of Hispanics said their household finances have suffered, while 10 per cent said they had improved.
TRANSGENDER SPORTS
Some 38 per cent of voters ahead of the election said keeping transgender girls and women out of women’s sports was a very important issue or the most important issue, compared to 25 per cent who said that about protecting the rights of transgender people.
What is on the table in today’s election?
So, with all the talk of midterms and a blue wave and a Democratic sweep seeing power seep away from Trump’s White House, it might be worth recapping just what is up for grabs today.
First things first. Congress has two chambers, the House of Representatives and the Senate.
The lower chamber, the House of Representatives, has 435 voting seats, each representing a district of roughly similar size. There are elections for each of these seats every two years.
The House has several exclusive powers, such as the power to initiate revenue bills, impeach federal officials and elect the president in the case of an electoral college tie.
The upper chamber, the Senate, has 100 members, who sit for six-year terms. A third of the seats come up for election in each two-year cycle. Each state has two senators, regardless of its population.
Most legislation needs to pass both chambers to become law, but the Senate has some important other functions, notably approving senior presidential appointments, for instance to the supreme court.
In most states, the candidate with the most votes on election day wins the seat.
However, Georgia and Louisiana require the winning candidate to garner 50 per cent of votes cast; if no one does, they hold a runoff election between the top two candidates.
Maine and Alaska use ranked-choice voting as opposed to the first past the post voting system in congressional elections.
Florida and Ohio are having ‘special elections’ for the Senate because the previous holders of their seats – Marco Rubio and JD Vance – resigned to join the executive branch following the 2024 presidential election.
And then there are governors.
They are elected by direct vote in their states. The candidate with the highest number of votes is declared the winner.
In every state, the executive branch is led by a governor. They serve for four years in office, with the exception of Vermont and New Hampshire where tenures are two years long.
Governors are responsible for implementing state laws, and have a range of powers available to them such as executive orders, executive budgets and legislative proposals and vetoes.
US voters go to the polls in election which could weaken Trump’s hold on power
Americans are heading to the polls today in US midterm elections widely seen as a referendum on Donald Trump’s second presidency and a chance for opponents to rein in his power.
The party holding the White House typically loses congressional seats at midterm elections and Democrats are hoping the president’s nose-diving popularity can be exploited.
Meanwhile, the US department of justice in California has charged six more people with alleged voter fraud crimes, an escalation of the administration’s campaign against election integrity.
However, in a blow to Trump, the supreme court has ruled against attempts to force California election officials to segregate and not count ballots from people the department claims are non-citizens.

sources.news_title: When do polls close and when will election results come in? A state-by-state guide to the 2026 midterms
sources.text:
When do polls close and when will election results come in? A state-by-state guide to the 2026 midterms
WASHINGTON (AP) — With voters deciding thousands of races across the country on Tuesday, keeping track of which races to watch throughout the night — and when to expect results — can get tricky.
Here’s a rundown of the biggest races hour by hour, along with some clues as to how long it will take to count the votes.
All times are in Eastern Standard Time.
6 p.m.
The first polls of the night will close in most of Indiana and Kentucky, but no statewide winners will be declared in either state until the last polls close at 7 p.m. It’s possible to see winners declared in the states’ easternmost congressional districts.
Key contests in this hour include competitive U.S. House races in Indiana’s 5th and Kentucky’s 6th congressional districts.
7 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.
All polls close at 7 p.m. in six states, including Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia, which tend to complete almost all of their vote counting on election night. In the 2024 general election, the vote count in all three states reached the halfway mark in the 8 p.m. hour. The counts were 90% complete at 10:21 p.m. in Georgia, 11:14 p.m. in South Carolina and 12:07 a.m. in Virginia. In Georgia’s competitive presidential contest, The Associated Press declared Republican Donald Trump the winner at 12:58 a.m.
Most Florida polls will also close at 7 p.m., including in every competitive congressional district, but no statewide winners will be declared until polls in the Central Time Zone close at 8 p.m.
Polls in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia close at 7:30 p.m. All three states also count votes relatively quickly, reaching the halfway point at around 9 p.m. in 2024 and about 90% in the 11 p.m. hour. The AP declared a winner in Ohio’s competitive 2024 U.S. Senate race at 11:27 p.m.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio; gubernatorial races in Georgia and Ohio; and U.S. House races in Florida, Indiana, South Carolina, Virginia, Ohio and North Carolina.
8 p.m. and 8:30 p.m.
The 8 p.m. hour is primetime on election night, with polls fully or partially closing in almost half the states, including key states like Florida, Maine, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania.
Florida tends to have one of the faster counts in this time slot, since results in most of the state start releasing in the 7 p.m. hour. In 2024, the Florida vote count was 90% complete by 8:07 p.m.
The 2024 vote counts in New Hampshire and Pennsylvania reached the halfway mark at 10:12 p.m. They reached 90% at 12:48 a.m. in Pennsylvania and 1:42 a.m. in New Hampshire.
Maine didn’t reach the halfway mark in 2024 until 12:54 a.m.
Polls in almost all of Michigan and Texas close at 8 p.m., including in the states’ most competitive congressional districts, but no statewide winners will be declared until the final polls have closed at 9 p.m.
Polls close at 8:30 p.m. in Arkansas.

9 p.m.
This is election night’s other big logjam, with all polls closing in 15 states, including the midterm battlegrounds of Arizona, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, Texas and Wisconsin.

Kansas, Michigan and Texas all begin releasing votes in the 8 p.m. hour, but Michigan trailed the other two in the 2024 vote count. Kansas and Texas reached 90% counted during the midnight hour, while Michigan didn’t reach that threshold until 4:50 a.m.
Although polls close in Arizona at 9 p.m., the state does not begin releasing results until 10 p.m.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska and Texas; gubernatorial races in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, Texas and Wisconsin; and U.S. House races in Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York and Wisconsin.
10 p.m.
Polls close at 10 p.m. in Montana, Nevada and Utah, with some polls closing in the eastern portions of Idaho and Oregon.
Key contests to watch in this hour include U.S. House races in Montana, Nevada and Utah and congressional and gubernatorial races in Arizona, where polls close at 9 p.m. but results are held until 10 p.m.

sources.news_title: US midterms 2026: Poll closing times, vote counting and when results are expected
sources.text:
Millions of Americans are heading to the polls on Tuesday, Nov. 3, as the United States prepares for a closely watched midterm election that could reshape the balance of power in Congress during President Donald Trump’s administration.
The election will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress or Democrats manage to win back one or both chambers. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are being contested.
While the first results are expected to emerge Tuesday evening, voters may have to wait hours, days or, in some closely fought races, longer to learn the final outcome. The time it takes to count ballots, state-specific voting rules and possible legal challenges can all affect when a winner is declared.
For voters following the results from outside the United States, including Indian Americans watching races across the country, understanding when polls close and how votes are counted is essential to making sense of election night.
When will U.S. midterm election results start coming in?
The first polling stations will close at 6 p.m. Eastern Standard Time (EST), or 4:30 a.m. Indian Standard Time (IST) on Wednesday, Nov. 4, in parts of Indiana and Kentucky.
Polls will close at different times across the country because the United States spans multiple time zones and some states have different closing times in different areas. As polling stations close, election officials will begin releasing vote counts.
However, the first numbers do not necessarily mean a winner has been decided. Election officials report results as ballots are processed, while news organizations such as The Associated Press analyze the available votes and other election data before declaring a race.
READ: List of Indian Americans to watch in the 2026 midterm elections (October 30, 2026)
In a closely contested election, the difference between candidates may be small enough that officials need to count additional ballots before the outcome becomes clear. As a result, a race may remain undecided well into Wednesday or beyond.
The larger question of which party will control the House and Senate may also take longer to answer, even if many individual races are called on election night.
What time do polls close across the United States?
The following schedule shows when polling stations are expected to close in different states. All times are listed in Eastern Standard Time (EST), followed by Greenwich Mean Time (GMT). Indian Standard Time is 5 hours and 30 minutes ahead of GMT.
6 p.m. EST: Parts of Indiana and Kentucky.
7 p.m. EST: Most of Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia, along with the remaining parts of Indiana and Kentucky and most of New Hampshire.
7:30 p.m. EST: North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia.
8 p.m. EST : Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, the remaining parts of New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee and Washington, DC. Polls also close in parts of Florida, Kansas, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota and Texas.
8:30 p.m. EST: Arkansas.
9 p.m. EST: Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming, along with the remaining parts of Kansas, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota and Texas.
10 p.m. EST: Montana, Nevada, Utah and parts of Idaho and Oregon.
11 p.m. EST: California and Washington, along with the remaining parts of Idaho and Oregon.
Midnight EST: Hawaii and most of Alaska.
1 a.m. EST: The remaining parts of Alaska, including the western Aleutian Islands.
These are poll-closing times, not deadlines for announcing winners. Vote counting and the release of results can continue after polling stations have closed.
Why could some states take longer to count votes?
Although many races may be decided relatively quickly, voting procedures differ from state to state. Mail-in ballots, signature verification, ranked-choice voting and rules allowing ballots to arrive after Election Day can all affect the timeline.
READ: Obama comes in support of Democrats ahead of midterm elections (October 25, 2026)
Here are some states where the counting process could take longer.
Alaska
Alaska uses ranked-choice voting in certain elections. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the first-choice votes, additional rounds of counting may be required to determine the winner.
The state also reports in-person early votes and Election Day votes on election night, while some mail-in ballot results arrive later. In 2024, about 75% of votes had been counted by the morning after Election Day, with the remaining ballots reported over the following days.
If Alaska’s Senate race requires another round of ranked-choice tabulation, the next round is scheduled for November 18.
California
California conducts much of its voting by mail. Election officials must receive, verify and process large numbers of ballots, and additional results can be released for days after Election Day.
In a close House race, these later counts could change the margin between candidates. As a result, it may take days or even weeks to determine the winner.
Arizona
In some Arizona counties, voters can drop off completed mail-in ballots on Election Day. Officials must verify signatures and process these ballots before counting them.
This means a substantial number of votes may remain outstanding after the first results are released, potentially delaying the outcome of closely contested races.
Nevada
Nevada mails ballots to registered voters. Mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive up to four days later under the state’s rules.
Voters also have six days after Election Day to address certain signature problems. These procedures can leave some ballots unresolved until the following week.
Maine
Maine, like Alaska, uses ranked-choice voting in certain elections. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the first-choice votes, officials may need to conduct additional rounds of counting.
For races that require this process, ballots are transported for further tabulation in Augusta, the state capital. This can delay the announcement of a final winner.
Washington
Washington conducts elections by mail. Ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive and be counted in the days that follow, meaning the initial results may not reflect the final vote totals.
Although individual races may be called on election night, the overall battle for control of Congress could remain unresolved while officials count the remaining ballots.
When will the final results be known?
There is no single deadline for announcing all the winners. The timeline depends on how close individual races are, how quickly ballots can be processed and whether recounts or legal disputes arise.
In races where one candidate has a clear lead, news organizations may be able to project a winner before every ballot has been counted. Official certification, however, takes place later through the election process established by each state.
The fight for control of Congress can be more complicated because a party must win enough individual races to secure a majority. Even if most results become clear on election night, a handful of undecided contests could determine which party controls the House or Senate.
The wait can be significant. In the 2024 election, it took eight days to determine which party would control the House of Representatives.
READ: Muhammad Ali’s family endorses Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan (November 2, 2026)
What happens if a candidate challenges the election results?
If a race is extremely close, a recount may be triggered automatically under state law or requested by a candidate who meets the applicable requirements. Candidates can also challenge election results in court, potentially extending the process.
The outcome of a challenge depends on the circumstances of the race, the evidence presented and the legal rules that apply. Recounts and court proceedings can take days, weeks or longer.
President Donald Trump has also raised questions about whether he would accept the results of the midterm elections. Asked whether he would respect the final outcome, Trump said, “I will if there are honest elections.”
However, the president cannot overturn congressional election results simply because he disagrees with them. Elections are administered and certified by individual states, and challenges must follow established legal procedures.
The U.S. Constitution also gives the House of Representatives and the Senate the authority to judge disputes concerning the elections and qualifications of their own members. This means that disputes involving congressional seats can involve both state-level election procedures and the relevant chamber of Congress.
Why do the midterm results matter?
The midterm elections will determine how much power Republicans and Democrats have in Congress during the remaining two years of Trump’s current presidential term.
If Democrats win control of either chamber, they could gain greater influence over legislation, government spending, investigations and congressional oversight of the administration. If Republicans retain both chambers, Trump would have a stronger chance of advancing his legislative agenda.
That is why the outcome matters beyond individual races. The results will shape the political environment in Washington and influence the decisions Congress makes before the next presidential election in 2028.
For now, the key thing to remember is that polls closing does not mean the counting is finished, and early results do not always determine the winner. While election night will offer the first indications of which party is gaining ground, the final balance of power may take several days to emerge.

sources.news_title: Election Day is here: Voters set to decide control of Congress
sources.text:
Election Day is here, with voters heading to the polls after a final campaign push across the country, including a closing message from President Donald Trump at Washington’s Reflecting Pool.
Plus, the U.S. launches new strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island just hours before Election Day, with officials calling the operation defensive even as Trump talks up the possibility of a diplomatic deal.
And the Supreme Court rejects a last-minute bid to set aside thousands of California mail-in ballots, delivering the Trump administration an Election Day setback without explaining its decision.
These stories and more highlight your Unbiased Updates for Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.
Election Day arrives with control of Congress up for grabs
After months of campaigning, Americans head to the polls to decide who controls Congress and the country’s direction for the next two years.
The final arguments have been made. Trump has delivered his closing pitch. And now, the decision belongs to the voters.
More than 57 million Americans had already voted before Election Day, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. That’s nearly as many as the total early vote in the 2022 midterms, with millions more ballots still to come.
And Monday night, Trump made his final appeal from Washington’s Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. He urged the voters who put him back in the White House in 2024 to turn out again to keep Republicans in control of Congress.
But he also acknowledged the history working against his party.
“Because if the people who voted for me and voted in the last election, where we had such a great victory, go out and vote- just a good portion of them — we will win in a landslide. Now, that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president, bad. For some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms. But we gave this a very strong shot.”
President Donald Trump
Vice President JD Vance spent his final day campaigning in Ohio, calling it the most important midterm election of his lifetime. He said he’s confident Republicans will hold Congress but acknowledged the outcome is no longer in their hands.
“I feel good about tomorrow, but obviously it’s in the hands of voters, so all I’d say is to remind the voters, particularly in Ohio, that Sherrod Brown is a career politician who spent 50 years in Washington delivering for Chuck Schumer. Jon Husted has delivered for the people of Ohio. I think they’re going to reelect him. But it’s up to the voters now.”
Vice President JD Vance
Across the country, some of the most consequential Senate races are entering their final hours. Here’s a look at the most contested races we are watching.
In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed closed their campaigns with appeals to a deeply divided electorate.
The race has exposed divisions within the Democratic Party after Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Rogers rather than her party’s nominee.
“It’s really about the heart and soul of the country and who we want to be and what country we want to give to our kids,” Rogers said. “And when you think about that, what happened is doors started opening for us. People knew something was wrong. Mean, angry divisiveness could not be the way in the future for our great state.”
Meanwhile, El-Sayed said he believes Americans have an opportunity to bridge gaps.
“And I believe that we have the opportunity to breach those divides: divides of geography, of race, of sexual orientation, gender identity, of faith, to build together what we can only have together,” El-Sayed said. “That’s what this campaign has been about from the very beginning. And while they think that somehow their intimidation tactics and their division are going to pull us apart, they don’t know us like we know ourselves. Royal Oak, when they come for us, we won’t back down.”
In Texas, where Republicans have dominated for decades, the Senate race has become a major test for both parties.
Democrat James Talarico said the Republican effort to defeat him shows how competitive the race has become.
“In the final days of this election, they are coming at us with everything they’ve got,” Talarico said. “The billionaire megadonors, the super PACs, are spending more than $300 million to try to stop us. That is the most of any Senate race in American history, and more is on the way. They are scared; they are terrified; they see what we see: that we’re about to win this election tomorrow night.”
Meanwhile, Republican Ken Paxton warned his supporters that the party’s grip on Texas is at risk.
“Texas has never been this close to slipping away,” Paxton said. “We have never been this close to losing everything we hold dear, our jobs, our livelihoods, our way of life in Texas. If Texas falls, we don’t have another Texas to move to. Every poll shows this is going to come down to the wire.”
In Alaska, the final days of the Senate race have been dominated by a controversy over two candidates with nearly identical names.
A New York Times report linked people working with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign and national Democrats to an effort to recruit another Dan Sullivan, the same name as the Republican incumbent.
The Senator accused his opponent of trying to mislead voters.
“My opponent has literally been caught in the biggest election-cheating scandal in Alaska history, and she is bleeding support,” Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan said. “People are pulling Peltola signs out of their yards, right? They are saying, ‘Hey, wait a minute, I did not sign up for corruption.’”
Peltola denies knowing about the effort and says she has no interest in tricking voters.
And in Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson is trying to unseat longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
His closing message focused on turnout and what he says voters can change in Washington.
“Up and down the state, people are showing up like I’ve never seen before, and that’s how we’re going to change this government. Together we can make so much of a difference. We can make so much of a difference here in the state. We can make so much of a difference in DC.”
Troy Jackson
The first polls close at 6 p.m. ET in parts of Indiana and Kentucky. From there, results will begin coming in across the country, with the final polls in Alaska closing at 1 a.m. ET Wednesday.
In some of these races, it could take longer to determine who won.
US launches new strikes on Iran after attack on American aircraft
Just hours before Election Day, the U.S. launched new airstrikes on Iran.
American officials said they launched defensive strikes, but the strikes come as Trump continues to talk about a possible deal with Tehran while threatening more military action.
U.S. officials said the military struck targets on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday near the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil shipments.
One official told ABC News the strikes were in response to an Iranian attack on an American aircraft. Officials said this was a limited operation, not the start of a new major offensive, but it’s not an isolated incident.
The U.S. has carried out other limited strikes in recent weeks as Iran has intensified attacks on commercial shipping in the strait. On Monday night, Trump was still raising the possibility of a much larger attack, this time on a suspected underground nuclear site known as Pickaxe Mountain.
“Now, we might have to go after Pickaxe, but that’s not a big deal,” Trump said. “We’ll do it in — literally, we can do that in one hour, okay? As soon as we want, at any time that we want.”
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard also claimed it shot down two American reconnaissance drones over Qeshm Island, but a U.S. official disputes the claim.
While both sides continue discussing a possible diplomatic deal, American forces are still carrying out strikes inside Iran.
Supreme Court blocks Trump’s California ballot bid
The Supreme Court has already dealt Trump a setback in his fight over California’s mail-in ballots. The justices rejected an emergency request from his administration Monday, just hours after it was filed.
The Justice Department wanted California to set aside ballots from more than 20,000 people it suspects are not U.S. citizens, but California officials question the list’s accuracy and warn that eligible voters could have their ballots wrongfully excluded.
The Supreme Court rejected the request in a one-sentence order without explaining its reasoning. No justices publicly dissented.
The decision follows a string of losses for the administration in lower courts. On Friday, a federal appeals court ruled 2-to-1 against the Justice Department’s request. The two judges in the majority wrote: “If the United States believes different procedures are necessary for vote-by-mail ballots, we believe it should take that suggestion to Congress, not the courts.”
The administration had argued that once the disputed ballots were mixed with other votes, they could not be separated. But the Supreme Court’s decision leaves California’s existing ballot-counting procedures in place for Tuesday’s election.
Questions linger over whether candidates will accept election outcomes
As voters head to the polls Tuesday, we’re also looking at what happens once the results start coming in and how candidates respond to them.
We caught up with our senior politics reporter, Azi Paybarah, outside the Capitol in Washington, D.C., to discuss what he’s watching for on election night and beyond.
CHRISTIAN BRYANT: What is it that you’re going to be watching for tonight, election night, and in the days that come? Whether it’s the races, whether it’s how candidates are reacting to the results. What are some of the things you’re going to be watching for?
AZI PAYBARAH: Big picture, I am looking at whether the mechanics of democracy go forward, or if anyone tries to interfere with it.
BRYANT: You said big picture. This feels like existential.
PAYBARAH: It is existential, and I do not mean it as hyperbole or a joke.
BRYANT: Can you break that down?
PAYBARAH: For 250 years, in sometimes very imperfect ways, people in the United States have elected representatives. Many people have lost elections. Many voters saw people they didn’t agree with take power and enact policies they opposed, yet society and the country still saw another day coming, another election, and this fight continuing.
Democracy wins if it continues, and the only way democracy loses is if it stops or if somebody changes the rules to make it ineffective.
What I am looking for is whether the president of the United States will keep arguing against moving democracy forward, and whether he will use the Department of Justice, the FBI and the weight of the federal government to interfere with election results he disagrees with.
I want to see how quickly news outlets call races. I’m also looking at voter turnout. How do candidates in Georgia do? But what I’m really looking at are the races that get called because of either blowouts or because the decision is just so clear, and whether candidates accept it.
And what I’m also watching is how the federal government, which has been very active in raising questions about election integrity, reacts. To call it an existential question is exactly correct.
BRYANT: When we think back to this midterm cycle, in the days and weeks and months and years to come, what will this cycle be remembered for?
PAYBARAH: Money. And whether or not the results are accepted. Now, I know in Alaska, the Mary Peltola campaign has been linked to an effort to bring in essentially a phony candidate.
BRYANT: She has denied part in it.
PAYBARAH: The thing that is sort of being lost in that conversation is just how frequently things like this happen. This isn’t the only campaign that’s ever been involved, or the only race that’s ever seen something like this.
BRYANT: Stacking the ballot as it’s called.
PAYBARAH: In fact, Mary Peltola’s own campaign, her own race, I believe two years earlier when she was running for re-election as a House member in Alaska, Republicans were linked to the effort to support a candidate running on that ballot who was a Democrat who was incarcerated.
BRYANT: So this happens.
PAYBARAH: This happens.
BRYANT: But I feel like there’s a but.
PAYBARAH: This happens. The “but” is always: do you get caught with your hand in the cookie jar, and is that cookie jar illegal, or is it just unethical?
BRYANT: Illegal cookies? Yay or nay?
PAYBARAH: If they’re illegal cookies, you’re in trouble. If they are merely unethical cookies, I have news for you. This is Washington. That’s considered the appetizer.
Investigators probe possible midair breakup after pilots reported icing and turbulence
Federal investigators said a private jet that crashed in South Florida, killing all nine people on board, may have been breaking apart before it hit the ground.
They’re now closely examining the severe weather the pilots encountered shortly before the crash.
The Learjet was flying from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas on Sunday when it plunged into a neighborhood near West Palm Beach — erupting in a massive fireball. Just minutes earlier, the crew reported ice buildup and turbulence at 35,000 feet. The pilots then declared an emergency as the plane rapidly descended.
The crash left a massive crater and scattered debris across the area.
Investigators said there’s evidence that parts of the jet may have broken off before impact.
“And as I indicated, we do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact. And so, some of this is yet to be determined. We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site.
I don’t think we’re far enough along here to know what we found. We’re finding debris, but we haven’t identified parts yet.”
Tom Chapman, National Transportation Safety Board
Recovering the wreckage is proving difficult, with much of it buried in the impact crater. About 600 nearby residents have been displaced. One person on the ground was injured.
Among the nine people killed were Texas businessman Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two young children, four-year-old Emma and two-year-old Charlie.
Investigators said it’s too early to determine what caused the crash.
Prosecutors seek retrial for Lindsay Clancy after 11-1 jury split
A second trial is taking shape for Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three young children. Prosecutors say they plan to retry her, but haven’t decided whether to pursue first-degree murder charges again.
Clancy returned to court Monday, two months after her first trial ended in a hung jury. Eleven jurors favored acquittal; only one voted to convict.
Her attorneys argue she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was not criminally responsible for the children’s deaths. Prosecutors say she knew what she was doing was wrong.
At Monday’s hearing, prosecutors also asked the judge to limit what attorneys can say publicly about the case, arguing that defense comments could influence a future jury. But things turned heated when Clancy’s lead attorney, Kevin Reddington, began questioning the conduct of the one juror who voted to convict.
Judge William Sullivan interrupted Reddington after he identified that juror by name.
KEVIN REDDINGTON: You don’t bring your background into a jury and suppress it, as was done in this case. This gentleman, Mr. (Michael Peguy) Desronvil …
JUDGE WILLIAM SULLIVAN: I’m going to — I’m going to stop you.
REDDINGTON: No, you’re not going to stop me.
SULLIVAN: I am.
REDDINGTON: No, you’re not.
SULLIVAN: All right. But, there is no need to bring out that juror’s name.
REDDINGTON: “It’s all over the internet.
SULLIVAN: That’s through the internet. That’s through other people. There’s no need here in this courtroom to use that.
The judge didn’t rule on the requests Monday. He’s considering a retrial as early as March, with another hearing scheduled for Nov. 16.
The defense has also asked him to dismiss the charges entirely, arguing that a second trial would violate double-jeopardy protections.
NASA’s Swift telescope heads home after nearly 22 years studying cosmic explosions
After nearly 22 years in space, a NASA telescope that spent its life observing some of the universe’s biggest explosions is about to make a fiery return to Earth.
The Swift observatory launched in 2004 to study gamma-ray bursts, among the cosmos’s most powerful explosions. But intense solar activity has pulled it closer to Earth, and a rescue attempt failed.
Still, it’s had quite a run.
Swift was only supposed to last two years. Instead, it made discoveries for nearly 22 years.
“It was designed for two years of science. Here we are almost 22 years later, able to answer questions that I think, you know, people at the start of the mission hadn’t even envisioned when it had started. And so I think the overwhelming sentiment is really one of appreciation, of gratitude, of pride in what we’ve been able to accomplish.”
Brad Cenko, principal investigator, Swift Observatory
Swift spotted more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars during its time in orbit.
NASA expects it to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere Wednesday, with most of the telescope burning up on the way down.
More from Straight Arrow:
Election results may be slow coming. Here’s why
News organizations flash blue and red check marks in a flurry of election night activity, calling races from one corner of the country to another. The behind-the-scenes work doesn’t have the same glamor. Election workers across 3,143 counties and thousands more cities and other local jurisdictions spend the evening and often several thereafter counting and curing ballots, finalizing and yes, even auditing their tallies. “Certified results” are often a blip on the radar weeks after confetti has been swept up.
So, why have elections over the last handful of cycles seen days, sometimes weeks, pass before some candidates can legitimately declare victory? What changed? The answer is as complicated as it is unsatisfying to most who hear it.
The U.S. has more than 210 million registered voters, split unevenly across the 50 states and the District of Columbia, each of which is responsible for running its own elections — and for the methods they use to tabulate results. They also maintain their own voter rolls, continually updated as voters move, die, re-register, enlist and get sent overseas. Millions just don’t vote.

ieExplains: US midterm elections key times and what's at stake
sources.text:
ieExplains: US midterm elections key times and what's at stake
Donald Trump has called it “most important in our lifetime” while senator Bernie Sanders says it’s the most important “in modern American history”.
Barack Obama called it a “circuit-breaker” and the “last, best chance” to rein in the president.
In any case, all eyes will be on the United States this week for the 2026 midterm elections.
Will Americans use the day as a referendum on Donald Trump’s second term? Will Democrats see a clean sweep of Congress?
Polls open at 11am Irish time in New York and other East Coast states and will continue in the rest of the US throughout the day.
Voting locations will begin to close 11pm Irish time tonight, with anybody still in line at that time eligible to cast a ballot.
A batch of US states will continue to close on the hour until 6am Irish time.
Many one-time Republican strongholds are up for the taking.
Election watchers will be laser-focused on Senate races for seats currently held by Republicans in Texas, Kansas, Maine, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska, as well as close races to hold on to Democratic seats in Michigan and Georgia.
Major names such as James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed are aiming for a win to flip red seats blue.
Every House seat, 435 of them, is up for re-election as sitting members are forced to defend their turf every two years.
And 39 governorships, powerful positions to lead states, are also up for election.
It depends. Some states report results quickly, while others are notoriously slow.
Many states are allowed to process absentee and mail-in ballots before election day so they can report a tranche of results soon after polls close. But some can’t. In short, here’s when some key races close on Wednesday in Irish time.
- 12am Georgia Senate
- 12:30am Ohio Senate
- 1am Maine Senate, Florida House
- 2am Kansas Senate; Texas, Iowa, Michigan Senate, House
- 6am Alaska Senate
Democrats tend to vote earlier in greater numbers and Republicans tend to vote more in person, so those early results can present a type of blue mirage that comes into sharper focus as the counts continue
What it will come down to is margin. If Democrats win a comfortable number of seats in the House, Senate or both, it could be an early result.
But if key races are tight, and the final breakdown of Congress comes down to a seat or two, the US – and keen onlookers the world over – could be in for a long week. Recent elections have seen some seats take hours to call, or even days.
Both chambers of the US Congress, the House and the Senate are in play.
If either switches hands it will be a major thorn in Trump’s side and sharply influence his agenda. If both do, he’ll be in peak lame duck territory.
The House is needed to pass any legislation, and has the ability to open investigations or demand testimony from Trump officials. A Democratic Senate could also stymie any nominations for positions such as the supreme court.
Many of those decisions come down to a simple majority vote.
But even with Democrats in charge, things such as impeachment remain relatively far-fetched as they need to meet a much higher barrier with a simple majority in the House but a two-thirds majority in the Senate.
Voters turn up and vote in person throughout the day which can present difficulties for anyone working a nine to five job. Polls generally close between 7pm and 9pm local time.
Election rules also differ in every state.
Some states allow early voting and some don’t.
Eight states mail ballots to all eligible voters, some allow mail-in ballots for absentee voting with no reason needed, while others require an excuse to request one.
Voters are also required to be registered to vote, and many states require that registration before election day.
Voter ID laws are also another barrier, with some states requiring a photo ID, some an ID with just a name and others no ID at all.
It’s a complex endeavour, and midterms usually see far fewer people vote than during presidential elections.
Turnout is generally between 40 to 50% of eligible voters, although early voting this year is significantly higher than during the last midterm election.

sources.news_title: Americans Vote In Midterm Elections To Upend Trump Presidency
sources.text:
Americans voted on Tuesday in pivotal midterm elections, with Democrats hoping to seize control of Congress and impose the first significant checks on Donald Trump’s chaotic second term in the White House.
If Republicans lose the House, Democrats could stall Trump’s legislative agenda and launch sweeping investigations into his administration. A Senate defeat would also threaten his ability to appoint Supreme Court justices and senior officials.
The election amounts to a nationwide judgment on Trump, with the mood turning sharply against Republicans amid anger over soaring living costs and the war against Iran.
All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are at stake, along with governorships in 36 states. Democrats need only three House gains and a net four seats in the Senate to wrest both chambers from Republican hands.
Trump returned to office last year promising to bring down prices, but inflation, tariffs, and fuel costs inflated by the Middle East conflict have squeezed Americans.
The 80-year-old’s approval rating has hovered near the low 30s.
In the suburbs of Atlanta, Georgia, retired teacher Jane Callum, 77, was among Democrats canvassing for Senator Jon Ossoff, who framed the race as a watershed moment for the country’s future.
“I really feel an obligation to do everything that I possibly can to change the direction that our country is going in now, and put it more on the path to democracy and away from autocracy,” she told AFP.
Economic discontent
Republicans insist that Trump’s tax cuts and immigration crackdown will benefit Americans, and they are portraying Democratic candidates as left-wing radicals.
But in his final public campaign appearance on Monday, Trump barely touched on the economy and spent most of the time in a rambling talk about his problem-plagued renovation of Washington’s Reflecting Pool.
“This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime,” he said, 26 minutes into the speech, before quickly returning to talking about renovations.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer branded it a “pathetic closing message.”
Some Republican supporters remain confident.
“We’re going to win. As a matter of fact, we’ve probably already won,” Texas military veteran Yvonne Clouser told AFP.
But while Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, the political battlefield is extending into conservative states like Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska.
Democrats must also defend competitive seats, including in Michigan, where a bitter internal dispute saw Congresswoman Haley Stevens endorse Republican Mike Rogers rather than the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.
Decision Desk HQ’s final forecast projected 241 House seats for Democrats against 194 for Republicans, and a narrower 52-48 Democratic Senate majority.
Disputed results?
Polls can underestimate one party’s support, and Republicans hope their voters turn out in force on Election Day.
More than 57 million Americans had already voted early before Tuesday, indicating the high energy.
The campaign has attracted more than $11 billion in political advertising, while mega-rich Trump ally Elon Musk has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican political efforts.
As soon as polls close, concerns will mount over whether results will be accepted by the Republicans.
Trump, who tried to overturn his 2020 election defeat, has repeatedly alleged widespread voter fraud and accused Democrats — with no evidence — of cheating.
The Justice Department, run by a close Trump ally, has already sued to potentially block certification of Alaska’s Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses, although a court ruled against the effort on the eve of the election.
And the Supreme Court rejected on Monday an emergency bid to force California to set aside the mail-in ballots of more than 20,000 people on the grounds that they may not be American citizens.
Trump, who will watch the midterm results at the White House on Tuesday night, signaled that if he does lose control of Congress, he could simply defy Democrats.
“I veto everything,” he told a podcast on Monday, although he said he might strike deals with Democrats eventually.
AFP

(The Center Square) – Polls are open in several eastern states as the final hours of the 2026 midterm elections begin and control of Congress hangs in the balance.
Several key states across the country are open for voting and will continue to accept voters until late in the night. The Center Square plans coverage of more than 80 races across the country on Tuesday night.
Here is a guide for when polls open and close across the country.
6 a.m. ET – CT, IN, Maine, KY, NY, NJ, VA, VT
Polls in Connecticut, Indiana, Maine, Kentucky, New York, New Jersey, Virginia and Vermont will be the first in the country to see voters at the polls on Election Day. Each state is in the Eastern time zone and accepts voters beginning at 6 a.m.

10 a.m. ET/ 7a.m. PT – CA, ID, NV, OR, WA
States along the West Coast and across the Pacific time zone will see polls open beginning at 7 a.m. A test of California’s redistricting in favor of Democrats will likely be top of mind for voters heading to the polls.
Poll openings in Washington and Oregon are subject to county-level discretion. Both states rely on mail-in voting to conduct elections. Polls will close in these states at 11 p.m. Eastern.
11 a.m. ET/ 7 a.m. AST – Alaska, NH
Alaska will see polls open at 7 a.m. Alaska Standard Time or 11 a.m. Eastern Standard Time. The crucial U.S. Senate race between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic candidate Mary Peltola will be key in control of the upper chamber in Congress.
Polls will not close in Alaska until 8 p.m. local time, or 1 a.m. Eastern time.
Additionally, while no specific time is listed, polls in New Hampshire must also be open by 11 a.m. ET on Election Day.
Noon ET/ 7 a.m. HST – Hawaii,
Hawaii will be the final state in the country to see polls open at 7 a.m. Hawaii Standard Time and Noon Eastern Time. Federal and statewide elections throughout the island will also contribute to control of Congress.
