sources.news_title: Trump faces crucial test as US votes for midterm elections
sources.text:
As Americans cast their ballots in the pivotal midterm elections, the outcome will determine the balance of power in the US Congress, serving as a critical referendum on Donald Trump's presidency and shaping the nation's political landscape for the next two years.
Key Points
- Americans began voting on Tuesday in midterm elections seen as a referendum on President Donald Trump's administration, marked by significant domestic and foreign policy challenges.
- The elections will decide control of all 435 House seats and 37 Senate seats, potentially shifting power from Republicans to Democrats and limiting Trump's legislative agenda.
- Several Indian-American candidates are contesting various posts, including Vivek Ramaswamy for Governor of Ohio and Nithya Raman for Mayor of Los Angeles.
- President Trump made a surprise announcement on polling day regarding US aid to Israel and campaigned extensively, while former President Barack Obama rallied support for Democrats.
- Democrats are aiming to flip seven Senate seats to gain a majority, despite a last-minute defection from Congresswoman Haley Stevens in Michigan.
Americans began voting on Tuesday in one of the most consequential elections in recent times, widely seen as a referendum on Donald Trump's presidency that has been marked by a prolonged war in Iran, rising inflation, trade wars and deep divisions in society.
On polling day, Trump sprung a surprise by announcing that the US will stop providing Israel USD four billion in aid from next year, which Democrat Ro Khanna described as a desperate attempt to stave off a "Blue tsunami".
The polling will decide whether President Trump's Republican Party retains control of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers of the US Congress, or, as opinion polls are predicting, the Democratic Party wrests control of at least the House if not the Senate, also in the final two years of Trump's second term in office.
Key Races And Congressional Control
Polling began on Tuesday at 6:00 a.m. eastern time in Indiana and Kentucky and in a staggered manner across time zones in the US. Polling began in California at 7:00 am local time (10:00 am Eastern) and in Alaska at 11:00 Eastern Time.
On the eve of the elections, the US launched limited strikes on Iran's Qesham island in the Hormuz Strait. Officials said that the strikes were in response to Iran firing at a US aircraft.
At stake in the elections are all 435 seats of the House and 37 seats in the 100-member Senate.
Elections are also being held for the post of Governor in 36 states, including in Ohio, where Indian American Vivek Ramaswamy is locked in a keen contest with his rival and Democratic nominee Amy Acton.
The first results are expected to trickle in from 5:00 am on Wednesday (India Time).
Indian-American Candidates In The Fray
A number of Indian American candidates are in the electoral fray for posts ranging from Governor to city council members. Democrat Nithya Raman, who was born in Kerala, is locked in a keen contest with her former boss Karen Bass for the post of Mayor of Los Angeles, the second-largest city in the US.
Indian-American lawmakers Ro Khanna, Ami Bera, Pramila Jayapal and Suhas Subramanyam are seeking re-election to the US House of Representatives, while fellow Democrats Pia Dandiya and Amish Shah are in the fray in competitive races to make their debut as Congresspersons.
Campaign Strategies And Political Stakes
On Monday, the Republicans and the Democrats made their final pitch to the voters, with Trump choosing an unusual venue  the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool  to focus on the renovations undertaken in the national capital instead of talking about tax cuts, tariffs and border security, which have been the high points of his election rallies.
According to the White House, Trump did a whirlwind tour of 20 states, mostly Republican strongholds, to address 30 rallies in the last 32 days. Analysts say his approval ratings are at an all-time low, and he has become a liability to Republican candidates.
If the pre-poll forecasts come true and Democrats take control of the US Congress, it will allow for deeper Congressional scrutiny and checks of Trump's actions, which will severely limit his ability to push his agenda. He will, however, retain the power to govern through executive orders, which will be valid for two years.
"We are reaching a boiling point in the country as a whole. There are the elites, the ruling class, the Epstein class that is truly 1 per cent that is wealthy, and there is the rest of us," Shuchita Patel, a Democrat, who is running for the post of Forsyth County Commissioner, told PTI.
Trump acknowledged the possibility of his wings being clipped but indicated that he will not allow Congress to slow him down.
"I guess I'll become Mr Veto," Trump told the New York Post's Pod Force One podcast in response to a question on Republicans losing control of both Houses of the US Congress, referring to the presidential power to veto actions by Congress.
Former President Barack Obama boosted the Democratic campaign with rallies in Ohio, Michigan and Georgia, which clearly left Trump rattled.
"This election is our last, best chance of at least reining him in, reining in some of the foolishness of this administration," Obama said in Georgia last week.
"It's the circuit-breaker in the system, and we need to flip it," he said, taking Trump to task for focusing on White House renovations instead of issues affecting the people.
The Battle For Senate Majority
The upbeat Democrats, however, suffered an unexpected setback in the eleventh hour when Congresswoman Haley Stevens of Michigan crossed over to the Republican side on Sunday, breaking ranks with Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who could be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
The Democratic Party quickly rallied behind El-Sayed by issuing statements condemning Stevens, who sprung a surprise by endorsing El-Sayed's Republican rival, Mike Rogers, and appearing alongside him in public.
Stevens lost in the Senate primary to El-Sayed. She is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the US ally.
The Democrats are hoping to flip seven Senate seats -- Michigan, Maine, Ohio, Kansas, Texas, Iowa and Alaska -- in their bid to gain a majority in the 100-member House.
Each of the 50 states in the United States is represented by two Senators who sit in the Congress for a six-year term. But the Senators are divided into three lots, and their terms are staggered so that elections are held every two years.
The House members are elected for a two-year term.
Republicans enjoy a majority in both chambers of Congress, but by thin margins.
In the House of Representatives, Speaker Mike Johnson has 218 Republicans and one independent, Kevin Kiley of California, against 214 Democrats, with two seats vacant.
The Senate is split 53-47 in favour of the Republicans. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to wrest control of the chamber. Of the 35 Senate seats are on the ballot, 22 are held by Republicans.
The mid-term elections are also crucial for Vice President J D Vance, who is burnishing his credentials to become a successor to Trump's mantle.
Vance made campaign stops in New York and Ohio on Monday, where Republicans were fighting for House and Senate seats.
He highlighted Trump's moves to end taxes on tips and overtime and secure the border while branding Democrats as "lunatics" who have contempt for American voters.
About 210 million Americans are registered to vote, according to USAFacts. California has the most registered voters, with 23.2 million, followed by Texas (17.4 million) and Florida (13.6 million). Together, they account for about 26 per cent of all registered voters.
Wyoming (278,468), Vermont (459,455) and Alaska (603,310) have the fewest.
According to the AP, more than 57 million ballots have been cast in 47 states and D.C. as of Monday, compared to a little under 44.5 million in 49 states and D.C. in 2022.

sources.news_title: U.S. voters hit polls as control of Congress hangs in balance
sources.text:
What to Know
- The first polls of the night have closed as Democrats and Republicans battle it out for control of Congress.
- All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot. Republicans entered Election Day with slight advantages in the Senate (53-47) and House of Representatives (219-214).
- But the GOP is at risk of losing control of both chambers. Nearly half of voters say they view the midterms as an opportunity for a major rebuke of President Donald Trump’s performance, according to early results from the NBC News Exit Poll.
- Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has won re-election against Republican Rep. Mike Collins, NBC News projects. It's a major hold for Democrats in one of the most closely divided battleground states.
- There are several other battleground Senate races to watch, including Abdul El-Sayed against Mike Rogers in Michigan, Ken Paxton against James Talarico in Texas, and Sen. Susan Collins against Troy Jackson in Maine.
- Gubernatorial races are taking place in 36 states, including California, Florida, Ohio and Texas.
- Voters are also deciding key ballot measures on abortion and transgender rights, redistricting and voter IDs.
Follow live updates below.
Democrat Josh Shapiro wins re-election in the Pennsylvania governor's race, NBC News projects
Democrat Josh Shapiro has defeated Republican Stacy Garrity to win another term in the Pennsylvania governor race, NBC News projects.
Polls close at 8 p.m. in 16 states and Washington, D.C.
Polls closed at 8 p.m. ET in more than a dozen states, including Senate battleground Maine, plus the District of Columbia.
Here are the states where polls closed at the top of the hour:
and Washington, D.C.
The next polls to close will be in Arkansas, at 8:30 p.m. ET.
NBC News Exit Poll: Voters are divided on transgender rights
Just over half of voters said that support for transgender rights in society has gone too far, according to early results from the NBC News Exit Poll. Twenty-five percent said support has not gone far enough and 22% said it has been about right.
This is broadly consistent with voters' views in 2024, when the AP VoteCast found 55% saying that support for transgender rights in government and society had gone too far.
When asked which party is better able to handle policies related to transgender people, voters gave Democrats a narrow 9-point advantage (44% to 35%), with 21% saying neither party is better. Views differed by gender, with women favoring Democrats on policies related to transgender people while men were split. Voters who said they didn't identify as male or female almost all either backed the Democratic Party (61%) or neither party (32%) on this issue.
Routine voting issues fuel conspiracy theories and confusion
Westchester County ballot tabulators malfunctioned across the county Tuesday, alarming voters and fueling a flurry of conspiracy theories online.
The issue was discovered early in the morning, after ballot tabulators failed to scan voters’ hand-marked paper ballots in 44 out of 45 of the county’s municipalities. State election officials said in a post on X that the issue was due to a programming error.
Election officials directed voters to put their ballots in secure orange ballot bags, following standard contingency plans.
The news has raised alarm amongst voters and onlookers. In text chains and Facebook posts viewed by NBC News, Westchester voters discussed the issue, with some expressing concern over whether their votes would be counted.
Tensions are high in part because Westchester is home to a key House race in the battle for control of Congress: in the 17th Congressional District, Republican Rep. Mike Lawler faces Democrat Cait Conley in a close race. The district narrowly leans blue, but Lawler has held it for four years by maintaining high popularity and campaigning aggressively on crime and affordability issues. Conley, a veteran and former Biden cybersecurity official, hopes to capitalize on the president’s sagging approval ratings in her challenge.
In social media posts, both candidates urged voters not to be dissuaded by the tabulator issues.
Ken Jenkins, the Westchester County Executive, said Tuesday afternoon that alternate tabulators are being rolled out, he said, and the ballots stored in secure bags will be counted after polls close at 9 p.m.
“Long-established emergency ballot procedures have been implemented, where completed ballots are secured, under bipartisan control, and will be counted,” the New York State Board of Elections said in a Tuesday statement posted on X. “While technical issues can be frustrating, contingency procedures exist for precisely these circumstances.”
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, told reporters that the ballots would be counted.
“Every vote will be counted; I think I need to say that three times. Every vote will be counted, every vote will be counted,” she said in Queens on Tuesday morning. “It’s being resolved in a bipartisan way that it’s supposed to. The backup plan is in place, so voters in Westchester should feel very confident.”
Isolated ballot scanner issues are routine, though the problems have been been particularly common in New York state. In 2018, scanners jammed across New York City, while Queens reported tabulator issues in 2024.
This year, ballot tabulator issues also occurred in other states including Florida and Oklahoma, while other issues like power outages and flooding shuttered some polling sites, including some in Maricopa County.
Online influencers supportive of the Republican party and some officials saw an opportunity in the malfunctioning machines and polling location closures, framing them as a conspiracy against party candidates.
“The Democrats are already cheating” posted Loomer Unleashed, a podcast associated with close Trump ally Laura Loomer, about power outages in Maricopa County. In reality, heavy rain and flooding have caused polling location issues across the county. The ballot counting issues in New York have sparked similar accusations, including from an elected official.
“The Democrats in NY will do anything and everything to cheat,” posted Rep. Claudia Tenner, R-N.Y., the chair of the House Election Integrity Caucus.
“Democrats are already trying to steal the election in New York today,” Loomer wrote on social media, her post garnering over 100,000 views.
“This is how the Left steals elections,” wrote Katie Miller, conservative podcast host and wife of White House advisor Steven Miller.
The nascent accusations echo similar narratives President Trump and his supporters raised in past elections. The most famous of these false narratives claimed machines stole votes away from Republicans, costing them the 2020 Presidential election. Yet technical failures are common, officials have warned, as are conspiracies about those malfunctions.
Researchers studying false online information have been worried about the potential for such accusations to recirculate as normal glitches get misrepresented. Such narratives could pave the way toward challenging the results of the election, several researchers told NBC News ahead of the midterms.
In Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, the county’s top election official said normal issues were getting far more attention than usual.
“It’s not uncommon to have some voting machines cause us a few problems early in the day. It’s a common occurrence,” said Doug Sanderson, the county’s election board secretary. “Many times we wouldn’t hear about it other than from our precinct officials, I just think perhaps the climate and the sensitive everyone has around this election causes people to be a little bit more on edge than they normally would be.”
Offline in Westchester County, voting at a Sleepy Hollow polling site at a social club called the Fraternal Order of Eagles appeared to be proceeding smoothly. A regular flow of voters trickled in and out through the lunch-hour in the Hudson River town, most having already heard via text message or from friends and neighbors that the scanners were not functioning.
As of 12:30 p.m ET, of the 225 people who had voted at that location, only two walked away on account of the tabulators being down.
“One was pretty disrespectful,” a poll worker named Dennis told NBC News, declining to share his last name. “The other said maybe they’d come back later.”
Democrat Jon Ossoff wins re-election in the Georgia Senate race, NBC News projects
Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has won re-election against Republican Rep. Mike Collins, NBC News projects, prevailing in Georgia after a nationally watched race that was defined, at times, by heated personal attacks.
Ossoff’s win is a major hold for Democrats in one of the most closely divided battleground states in the country — and one that both sides saw as critical for control of the Senate earlier this election cycle. Ossoff grabbed an early advantage in the race and held on, with a massive money advantage and a sizable lead in most public polling.

sources.news_title: Everything to know about the US midterms as Trump's future hangs in the balance
sources.text:
American voters have the chance to make or break Donald Trump’s presidency on Tuesday, with midterm elections taking place across the United States.
They will decide the makeup of the US Congress, with hundreds of seats being contested across the House of Representatives and the Senate. This will determine how easily Trump can pass his political agenda and how much scrutiny his administration faces.
Elections will be also be held for state assemblies and governors, city mayors, councillors, officials and even judges.
But the vote is often viewed as a de facto referendum on the sitting president – and it isn’t looking good for Trump.
Shorts
The midterm elections take place every two years, in the middle of a president’s four-year term of office. This year, all 435 members of the House will be elected for two-year terms. In the Senate, 35 of 100 seats are up for election, for six-year terms.
In the House, Republicans currently hold 218 seats to the Democrats’ 214. There is one independent member and two vacancies. In the Senate, the Republicans have 53 seats compared with the Democrats’ 45 – although two independents caucus with the Democrats.
Current polling suggests the Democrats are likely to win the House of Representatives, and have a good chance of winning the Senate, with some suggestions these could be the worst midterm elections for any president, ever.
Data-modelling site Race to the White House gives the Democrats a 94 per cent chance of taking the House and a 76 per cent chance of winning the Senate. An NBC News survey conducted in the final days of October found Democrats generally ahead by 52 per cent to 45 per cent across the country.
Another poll found Democrats beating Republicans in nearly all of the seven battleground states that will determine who controls the Senate.
This is largely down to the soaring cost of living, which has been exacerbated by Trump’s war with Iran, and consistently polls as the top issue for voters.
Dr Jonny Hall, a US foreign policy lecturer at the London School of Economics, said the midterms were “traditionally seen as a kind of referendum for the first half of a presidential administration”, especially if one party has controlled the presidency, the Senate and the House of Representatives – as has been the case for the last two years.
“The general pattern is very clear; incumbent governments tend to lose congressional seats in these elections,” Hall said. “As such, it is normally harder for presidential administrations to govern in the last two years of their term – congressional oversight may grow, and Congress, vitally, has the power of the purse which it can use to extract concessions.”
What could the election mean for Trump?
The midterms “are likely to signal the end of the second Trump presidency”, according to Professor Bill Durodie of the University of Bath.
“It would mean that, for the remainder of his presidency, he would effectively be a lame-duck president, unable to pass his policies into action.”
Greater Democratic power in Congress could make it “very painful for the President to push through their agenda”, and could trigger more investigations into potential corruption and abuse of power in the Trump administration, according to Natasha Lindstaedt, a professor of government at the University of Essex.
With greater power in the House, the Democrats might also bring forward impeachment hearings focused on both the President and his cabinet officials. If the party takes the Senate, it could block any further nominations to the Supreme Court, America’s highest judicial authority, and other Trump appointees.
David Andersen, associate professor of US politics at Durham University, said Trump had “never relied on Congress to enact his agenda, and instead has always preferred to rely upon executive actions” – but a united Congress might be able to block some of his policies.
“We could see his tariffs rolled back, and the cuts to government agencies blocked,” Andersen suggested. “Democrats may also almost certainly attempt to stop Trump from his various development projects on federal land, such as the White House ballroom and the ‘Triumphal Arch‘.”
A strong midterms showing will also help set up the Democrats for the next presidential election – especially with a large majority. “Within the House, any majority is sufficient to control the chamber, but if the Democrats’ majority stretches to 20 or 30 seats, this provides them the comfort of being able to allow members in competitive seats to break from party-line voting if it will help their future electoral chances,” Andersen said.
However, the White House already appears to be preparing a Plan B. Trump has reportedly already made plans on how to govern with a minority government by focusing on policy areas that can be pursued without legislative approval, and he could well use the presidential veto for legislation which he does not approve of.
Some analysts fear that a painful midterm result could make Trump more impulsive on the international stage, where the presidency has greater power. “The only area that Trump will be left with unfettered control is foreign policy, and that could be where he tries to establish a legacy,” Andersen said.
A senior Ukrainian source told The i Paper that a bad election result “could make Trump more impatient” and that “a Ukraine deal is among very few wins he can deliver on his own”.
With the US President having already proven willing to entertain the Kremlin’s maximalist peace demands, and considering his continued hostility to the Ukrainian President, Volodymyr Zelensky, the source feared that Trump could force Kyiv into a peace deal in which it loses land or security.
Trump has also threatened to resume attacks on Iran, saying this week that he would use a “hammer” on Tehran. Some reports have suggested this could go as far as a nuclear strike, with right-wing US media personality Tucker Carlson claiming that Israel was putting pressure on the White House to consider using nuclear weapons.
Trump denied this month that he would use nuclear weapons against Iran, but said he was considering using a devastating conventional weapon, the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, known as the Moab, or “mother of all bombs”, against Iranian nuclear sites.
Races to watch
Some of the most revealing political battles have been taking place in the contest for the Senate, Andersen said, with Republicans “in tight races in places that they should not be” throughout the Midwest, including in Iowa, Kansas, and Nebraska, where Republicans would normally enjoy double-digit leads.
“If the polls are correct, Republicans could be in for a shocking and historic loss,” Andersen said. “Even if the polls are wrong and Republicans do better than expected, they are still likely to have a very bad night. The best hopes for the GOP [Republican Party] right now seem to be that they might be able to win some close races and maintain a 50-50 split in the Senate, with Vice President [JD] Vance serving as the tie-breaker.”
Michigan and Texas are two key states to watch, according to Lindstaedt. “A win for the Democrats in Michigan will show the Democrats that a progressive [Abdul El-Sayed] can win, and a win in Texas would show the breadth of the Democratic brand,” she said, but added: “Everything would need to go the Democrats’ way, because these races are all really tight.”
But a resounding Democratic victory might not spell the end of the process. After Trump falsely claimed the 2020 presidential election had been rigged – a move that triggered his supporters to storm, smash and loot the US Capitol building in January 2021 – there are concerns that he may not accept a negative result.
He could decide to declare a national emergency, seizing voting machines and electronic voting records from unspecified polling locations, claiming the move was justified because of alleged fraud, Lindstaedt said – though these actions would most probably be found unlawful in court.
Trump and his Justice Department could also file lawsuits to try to prevent Republican losses, as he has done in Alaska – although this has now been tossed out by a judge – or encourage Republican candidates or other allies to file their own challenges.
“This could lead to a lot of delays in certification and in getting the results, which will cause tension if the blue wave [a huge Democrat victory] is not as big as predicted,” Lindstaedt said.
While Trump does not appear to be moving forward with some of his more extreme threats, such as sending troops to “secure the polls”, it is possible that he will urge his supporters not to accept an electoral loss, Andersen added.
“This could lead to more violence, like what we saw on 6 January, 2021,” Andersen said.
“Given his weak approval ratings, and following on the heels of a potential Democratic landslide, this could make Trump the least popular president in history, and effectively prematurely end his ability to govern at all.”

Americans head to the polls on Tuesday to decide whether Donald Trump’s second presidency will continue with Republican control of Congress or face a powerful Democratic opposition, as the party seeks to take control of the House and challenge Republicans in the Senate.
A Democratic victory in the House would give the party the ability to block parts of Trump’s legislative programme and launch investigations into his administration.
Losing the Senate would also complicate the president’s efforts to secure confirmation for Supreme Court justices and other senior government appointments.
The midterm elections have become a nationwide test of Trump’s leadership, with Republicans facing growing public dissatisfaction over the rising cost of living and the war with Iran.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are being contested, alongside governorships in 36 states. Democrats need to gain three seats in the House and secure a net gain of four in the Senate to take control of both chambers.
Trump returned to the White House last year promising to lower prices, but persistent inflation, tariffs and higher fuel costs linked to the Middle East conflict have added to financial pressures on households.
The 80-year-old president’s approval rating has remained close to the low 30s.
In suburban Atlanta, Georgia, retired teacher Jane Callum, 77, was campaigning for Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff. She described the election as a critical moment for the country’s future, telling AFP that she felt compelled to help redirect the United States towards democracy and away from what she viewed as authoritarian rule.
“I really feel an obligation to do everything that I possibly can to change the direction that our country is going in now, and put it more on the path to democracy and away from autocracy,” she said.
Republicans have defended Trump’s economic policies, arguing that tax cuts and tougher immigration enforcement will benefit Americans. They have also sought to portray Democratic candidates as far-left politicians.
However, during his final public campaign appearance on Monday, Trump devoted little attention to the economy. Much of his speech focused on the troubled renovation of Washington’s Reflecting Pool.
He described the midterms as potentially the most important in a generation, but quickly returned to discussing the renovation project.
“This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime,” he said.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer criticised the speech, describing it as a poor final campaign message.
Some Republican supporters remain confident of victory. Texas military veteran Yvonne Clouser told AFP she believed the party would win and might already have secured the result.
Although Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate, Democrats are seeking gains in traditionally conservative states, including Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska.
The Democrats also face difficult contests in states where they must defend vulnerable seats. In Michigan, an internal party dispute heightened after congresswoman Haley Stevens backed Republican candidate Mike Rogers instead of the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.
Decision Desk HQ’s final projections gave Democrats 241 seats in the House against 194 for Republicans. Its Senate forecast was much closer, predicting a 52-48 Democratic majority.
Although opinion polls can misjudge voter support, Republicans are counting on strong turnout from their supporters to improve their chances on election day.
More than 57 million Americans had already cast ballots before Tuesday, reflecting significant early participation.
The campaign has attracted more than $11 billion in political advertising, while billionaire Elon Musk, a prominent Trump ally, has committed hundreds of millions of dollars to Republican political efforts.
Attention is also turning to whether Republican leaders will accept the results if their party loses control of Congress.
Trump has repeatedly questioned the integrity of US elections and made unsupported claims of widespread voter fraud. He also sought to overturn his defeat in the 2020 presidential election.
The Justice Department, led by a Trump ally, has already taken legal action that could have prevented certification of Alaska’s Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan lost by a narrow margin. A court rejected the effort on the eve of the election.
The Supreme Court also turned down an emergency request on Monday seeking to prevent California from counting the mail-in ballots of more than 20,000 people whose citizenship had been questioned.
Trump, who will watch the midterms results at the White House on Tuesday night, signaled that if he does lose control of Congress he could simply defy Democrats.
In a podcast interview on Monday, he said he would veto everything, although he indicated that he could eventually negotiate agreements with Democrats.
